title: [MNT]: ListedColormap inconsistencies
body: ### Summary  The documentation to `ListedColormap` states that the input should be a list or array https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/blob/b01462c9ac7b0d3875892d6f40c9213c56f0864f/lib/matplotlib/colors.py#L1175-L1177  However, when specifying *N*, `str` and `float` are also supported (if one use the source code) https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/blob/b01462c9ac7b0d3875892d6f40c9213c56f0864f/lib/matplotlib/colors.py#L1199-L1214  This means that, e.g., `ListedColormap("#aabbcc", N=1)` works, but `ListedColormap("#aabbcc")` does not (there will be weird errors later, like `N=7` for the latter). Given that there is `monochrome` attribute and the documentation of *N*, one may expect the latter to work as well (if the earlier works). Also, `ListedColormap(["#aabbcc"])` will not set the `monochrome` attribute correctly.  ### Proposed fix  I think there are three(?) possible solutions: * Support scalars/strings when *N* is not provided (and ideally documents that) * Document that if *N* is not None, the first argument can be a scalar or string (it is maybe easier to do `ListedColormap(0.3, N=7)` than `ListedColormap([0.3]*7)` or at least require slightly less Python knowledge) * Deprecate scalar/string argument  Bonus: document the `color` and `monochrome` attributes

title: [ENH]: Specifying figure size based on width and ratio/aspect
body: ### Problem  While playing around with style files, I realize that for a paper it often makes sense to specify the width (set by the publisher) and ratio (determined by what we plot). Although one can of course read up and remember the figure width etc, it is quite convenient to just use a style file to determine the width and then set the ratio when creating the figure.  ### Proposed solution  There is https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.figure.Figure.set_figheight.html so one way is of course to create the figure using the style file and then set the height suitably.   However, some options are:  `set_figratio`, basically: ``` python set_figheight(self.get_figwidth()*ratio) ```  Add a `figratio` keyword to Figure (and subplots and figure and ...) that takes the width, either from `figsize` or add a new rcParam for figwidth. Not sure which is less confusing...  (I think one can argue that the width should be kept when modifying the ratio based on the publisher-defined argument.)  Edit: searching a bit more I found https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/figure_api.html#matplotlib.figure.figaspect which does the exact opposite to what I want. Maybe an option is to come up with a good name for a similar function that determines the size with fixed width? Although the original idea was to make it "simple".

title: [ENH]: Possible improvements for out-of-the-box interactivity
body: ### Problem  Compared to other visualization frameworks, matplotlib has very limited capability for interacting with the plot. I think we could do a bit better here.  There are two obstacles related to interactivity in Matplotlib: 1) By design, we have a one-way processing pipeline from data to a visual representation (pixels or vector primitives). Backtracking which data or Artist is responsible for a visual output is possible, but not quite easy. Additionally, any desired visual change requires a complete re-rendering. 2) We have multiple backends and want to provide consistency. This means, we have non-interactive backends that just can't provide interactivity. The interactivity we provide should work across all interactive backends.  1 is an architecture limitation, that we cannot easily circumvent. This means, we won't be high-perfoming and won't be able to support complex interactions. 2 also limits the complexity of interactions we can practically implement. OTOH it does not mean we cannot provide any interactivity at all. For example, we do have panning and zooming in interactive backends.  ### Proposed solution  Let us consider which small improvements we can reasonably make to improve interactive experience. The following list should track interactivity ideas that seem prossible to implement under the current architecture with limited effort. Please feel free to add:  - [ ] Data tooltip support #23378 - [ ] Support panning and zooming using mouse scroll wheel #20317 - [ ] Toggling data via legend #16796

title: DOC: Best practice when to use ax.set_thing(foo) vs ax.set(thing=foo)
body: ### Documentation Link  _No response_  ### Problem  Inspired through the discussion at https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/pull/28677#discussion_r1708863650: Through #20569 we have made `Artist.set()` more useable. In particular, we have started to `Axes.set()` in some places in the documentation.  We currently do not have a best practice when to `ax.set_thing(foo)` vs `ax.set(thing=foo)`.  ### Suggested improvement  We should have a best practive when to use what that we document, teach and use in our docs.  There was a loose discussion at https://github.com/matplotlib/ProjectManagement/blob/b9b0a56cb7b329c3c2adfac77a84975f70868e24/meeting_notes/2021/q2.md#do-we-want-to-soup-up-and-advertise-objset-more, but no definitive solution.  General observations: - Both APIs are intended to co-exist. We don't plan to get rid of one or the other. - Advantages of `set_thing()`:   - more specific   - easier to find the docs (for `set(thing=...)` one has to go to `set()` and follow the link for the specific keyword).   - more functionality through kwargs available - Advantages of `set(thing=...)`:   - shorter - Neutral   - tab completion should work for both cases (`ax.set_<TAB>` and `ax.set(<TAB>`)   - API is fully documented for both cases (no more `set(**kwargs)` signatures)   - Historically `set_thing` was mostly used and advertized    Please add if you have additional points.  I'll stop here without suggesting a solution to keep the discussion unbiased. Suggestions for solution should be posted as separte comments.

title: [MNT]: Move norms to from colors.py to separate file norms.py
body: ### Summary  Currently the data→norm→color pipeline involves two files: 1. `colors.py`:     1. Utility functions for working with colors     2. `Colormap` and subclasses of `Colormap`      3. `Normalize` and subclasses of `Normalize` 2. `cm.py`:     1. The colormap registry     2. `ScalarMappable` (holds data, norm and colormap)  In this structure, each file contains multiple parts of the pipeline, and it is not intuitive which part of the pipeline is located where.  With PR #28658 we are creating `colorizer.py` and the new `Colorizer` object to improve the data→norm→color pipeline. This has the added benefit that it greatly simplifies `cm.py`, which now only contains the colormap registry (and ScalarMappable for compatibility reasons).   ### Proposed fix  This issue suggests moving the norms to a separate file in order to clean up `colors.py`. This, together with  #28658 would lead to the following structure:  1. `colors.py`:     1. Utility functions for working with colors     2. `Colormap` and subclasses of `Colormap`  2. `norms.py`     1. `Normalize` and subclasses of `Normalize` 2. `cm.py`:     1. The colormap registry 3. `colorizer.py`     1. `Colorizer` (handles the data→norm→color pipeline)  With this structure, each file only contains a single part of the pipeline.   This issue came up because I was looking to implement multivariate color mapping (see issue #14168, and PRs #28454, #28658, [#28428]) , and for this we will need at least one more norm (i.e. `MultiNorm`).

title: BUG: Series/DataFrame.replace with a callable value silently stores the function instead of applying or rejecting it
body: Passing a callable as `value` to `replace` stores the function object as the replacement data. It neither applies it nor raises:  ```python s = pd.Series(["a1", "b2"]) s.replace(r"\d", lambda m: "X", regex=True) # 0    <function <lambda> at 0x...> # 1    <function <lambda> at 0x...> ```  Same for exact match without regex and for `DataFrame.replace`. Reproduced on 3.0.5.  `Series.str.replace` with the same arguments returns `["aX", "bX"]`, and the `replace` docs list `value` as scalar/dict/list/str/regex with no callables. GH#18634 set the precedent that invalid `replace` arguments raise, and the suite tests a callable `to_replace` raising, but nothing covers a callable `value`. On main (`pandas/core/generic.py`, `replace`), `to_replace` is validated up front and `value` is not checked at all.  The corruption spreads silently: the result is object dtype holding functions, `to_json` renders them as `{}`, and later string ops fail far from the mistake (`TypeError: expected string or bytes-like object, got 'function'`). Support callables or raise like `to_replace` does. Storing them should not happen.

title: BUILD: window/meson.build never passes --shared=pandas._libs._cyutility to its extensions
body: `pandas/_libs/window/meson.build` opens with  ```meson cy_args = ['-X always_allow_keywords=true'] # Use shared utility code to reduce wheel sizes # copied from https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/31151/files if cy.version().version_compare('>=3.1.0')     cython_args += ['--shared=pandas._libs._cyutility'] endif ```  but both `py.extension_module` calls in that file pass `cython_args: cy_args`. The `+=` lands on `cython_args`, the variable inherited from `pandas/_libs/meson.build` (which already appends the same flag there), so the flag never reaches `pandas._libs.window.aggregations` or `pandas._libs.window.indexers` — each of them still emits its own copy of the Cython utility code. The append also mutates the inherited variable as a side effect, which is not what the surrounding code intends.  `cy_args` is also missing the `--include-dir` pair that `pandas/_libs/meson.build` puts in `cython_args`.  Introduced by GH-61384 (341f1612a98). Impact is wheel size only — no correctness effect.  Fix: pass the shared flag to the window extensions, e.g. append to `cy_args` rather than `cython_args` (or reuse the parent `cython_args` directly if the `--include-dir` entries are wanted here too).

title: BUILD: pyproject.toml banned-api comment is wrong — TID251 does resolve np.random through the alias
body: `pyproject.toml` carries this in `[tool.ruff.lint.flake8-tidy-imports.banned-api]`:  ```toml # numpy.random is banned but np.random is not. Is this intentional? # "numpy.random".msg = "Do not use numpy.random" ```  The premise is false. TID251 resolves qualified names through aliased module imports, so with `import numpy as np` a `"numpy.random"` entry does flag `np.random.rand()` at the call site. Verified against ruff 0.15.7 and the pinned 0.16.1:  ```toml [tool.ruff.lint.flake8-tidy-imports.banned-api] "numpy.random".msg = "no np.random" ```  ```python import numpy as np np.random.rand()   # -> TID251 `numpy.random` is banned ```  So either the commented-out entry can simply be uncommented — pandas already forbids unseeded `default_rng()` / `np.random` in tests via a pygrep hook in `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, which this would partly subsume — or, at minimum, the misleading comment should be deleted so nobody re-derives it.

title: TST: pandas/tests/api/test_api.py::TestApi::test_api fails when that directory is run on its own
body: `TestApi.allowed_api_dirs` in `pandas/tests/api/test_api.py` lists `"internals"`, and `test_api` compares that list against `dir(pandas.api)`. But `pandas/api/__init__.py` does not import the `internals` submodule, and a submodule only shows up in its parent's `dir()` once something has imported it. So the test passes only when an earlier test in the same process has done that — in practice `pandas/tests/internals/test_api.py`.  Run the directory on its own and it fails:  ``` $ pytest pandas/tests/api/test_api.py -p no:randomly FAILED pandas/tests/api/test_api.py::TestApi::test_api - AssertionError: Iterable are different  Iterable length are different [left]:  6 [right]: 7 [diff]: ['internals'] ```  ```python import pandas as pd "internals" in dir(pd.api)   # False import pandas.api.internals "internals" in dir(pd.api)   # True ```  `pandas/api/internals.py` exists and is tracked; this is purely about whether it has been imported.  Not a CI risk today (CI runs the whole suite), but it makes running that one directory locally look broken, and the test is only green because of what its neighbours happened to do first.  Fix is one of:  1. import `internals` from `pandas/api/__init__.py` — it is public API, so arguably `pd.api.internals` should be reachable off a bare `import pandas`; 2. import it in the test before checking; or 3. drop it from `allowed_api_dirs` and assert it separately.  Choosing between them is really a question about whether `pd.api.internals` is meant to be reachable without an explicit import.

title: BUG: validate_test_dependencies.py is blind to pixi [target.*.dependencies]
body: `scripts/validate_test_dependencies.py` (pre-commit hook `validate-test-dependencies`) checks that every module gated by `pytest.importorskip` / `td.skip_if_no` is installed in at least one pixi environment that runs the test suite.  `declared_packages` builds that set from `pixi["dependencies"]` plus, per environment, `pixi["feature"][f]["dependencies"]` and `["pypi-dependencies"]`. It never reads the top-level `[target.<platform>.dependencies]` tables. `pixi.toml` has one today:  ```toml [target.win.dependencies] tzdata = ">=2023.3" ```  So a gate on a platform-scoped dependency gets reported as  ``` 'tzdata' gates tests with importorskip/skip_if_no, but 'tzdata' is not installed in any environment that runs the test suite, so these tests never run: ```  which is false as written — it *is* installed, on Windows. There is no such gate on main right now, so this is latent rather than currently firing, but it will fire the moment someone adds one, and the failure mode is a pre-commit hook telling the author something untrue about their own diff.  The underlying warning is still worth having: a Windows-only gate does mean the test is skipped on every Linux and macOS job, which is usually not what the author intended. So the fix is probably not to silence it but to parse the `[target.*.dependencies]` tables and reword — report *which* platforms the gate actually runs on, rather than claiming none. Distinguishing "runs nowhere" from "runs only on win" is the useful signal, and only the first should fail the hook.  No false negatives, only a misleading message on what is arguably a true positive.

title: PERF: avoid per-element group labels in nullable DataFrame axis=1 reductions
body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  The existing `axis=1` reduction path for homogeneous ExtensionArray-backed DataFrames concatenates the columns into a one-dimensional array. It then constructs the row labels with:  ```python row_index = np.tile(np.arange(nrows), ncols) ```  This creates one group label for every element in the DataFrame. The flattened values and labels are subsequently passed to `_groupby_op` with `ngroups=nrows`.  For supported nullable masked and Arrow numeric or Boolean arrays, the existing groupby kernels can instead operate on column-major data and mask buffers viewed as `(nrows, ncols)`. The specialized path requires only `ncols` zero-valued group IDs and one group. This retains the kernel and the ordering of columns within each row while avoiding the `nrows * ncols` label allocation.  The optimization applies to `sum`, `prod`, `min`, and `max`. Unsupported ExtensionArrays, Arrow subclasses and types, other operations, and empty DataFrames continue to use the existing path. Arrow numeric and Boolean arrays delegate through their corresponding masked representation before the result is reconstructed as an Arrow array. Public behavior is intended to remain unchanged.  The following reproducer uses four nullable integer columns, 100,000 rows, and approximately 10% missing values:  ```python from timeit import repeat  import numpy as np import pandas as pd   rng = np.random.default_rng(2) values = rng.integers(-100, 100, size=(100_000, 4)).astype(float) values[rng.random(values.shape) < 0.1] = np.nan df = pd.DataFrame(values).astype("Int64")   def best_ms(func):     return min(repeat(func, number=20, repeat=7)) / 20 * 1_000   print(f"pandas: {pd.__version__}") f

title: PERF: avoid temporary allocations in multi-block DataFrame axis=1 reductions
body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.   ## Reproducible Example  Multi-block `DataFrame` reductions along `axis=1` use the `_reduce_axis1` fast path for operations such as `sum`, `prod`, `min`, and `max`. There’s some concern about the deprecation path for that  At the moment the `_reduce` method by default already dispatches to the reduction methods if they are implemented: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/964b99e97a9856a66fdec90f8eede7d9a6301324/pandas/core/arrays/base.py#L2478-L2483  From that a possible deprecation path could be to implement the reduction methods (raising `TypeError` or `NotImplemented` by default). title: BUG: IntervalDtype.__from_arrow__ ignores the struct-level validity bitmap
body: ### Reproducible Example  ```python import numpy as np import pandas as pd import pyarrow as pa  st = pa.struct([("left", pa.float64()), ("right", pa.float64())]) arr = pa.array([{"left": 0.0, "right": 1.0}, None], type=st) pd.IntervalDtype(np.dtype("float64"), "right").__from_arrow__(arr) # <IntervalArray> # [(0.0, 1.0], (0.0, 0.0]] # Length: 2, dtype: interval[float64, right] ```  ### Issue Description  The second entry is null in the arrow array but reads back as `(0.0, 0.0]` instead of NA.  `IntervalDtype.__from_arrow__` reads only `arr.field("left")` / `arr.field("right")`. pyarrow's `StructArray.field()` does not merge the parent struct's validity bitmap into the child, so a null struct entry whose children are non-null is read as whatever the children hold (typically 0).  This is not reachable from pandas-written data: `IntervalArray.__arrow_array__` nulls both the child values and the struct-level bitmap, so `np.asarray(child)` recovers the NaN. Only externally-produced arrow data trips it.  The fix is to apply `arr.is_valid()` (or use `arr.flatten()`, which does apply the parent bitmap) before building the `IntervalArray`.  Found while working on GH-64297.  ### Expected Behavior  The second interval is NA.

title: BUG: IntervalArray.__arrow_array__ rejects ExtensionDtype subtypes, and ArrowIntervalType metadata cannot round-trip them
body: ### Reproducible Example  ```python import pandas as pd import pyarrow as pa  ser = pd.Series(pd.IntervalIndex.from_breaks(pd.date_range("2012", periods=5, tz="Europe/Brussels"))) pa.array(ser) # TypeError: Conversion to arrow with subtype 'datetime64[us, Europe/Brussels]' is not supported ```  ### Issue Description  `IntervalArray.__arrow_array__` computes the arrow subtype with `pyarrow.from_numpy_dtype(self.dtype.subtype)`, which raises for any `ExtensionDtype` subtype — including `DatetimeTZDtype`, which `IntervalArray` otherwise supports.  GH-64297 fixed only the read side (`IntervalDtype.__from_arrow__`), so an interval-with-tz column can now be read from arrow but still cannot be written.  Lifting the restriction is not just a subtype-lookup change: `ArrowIntervalType.__arrow_ext_serialize__` stores `str(self.subtype)` and deserializes with `pyarrow.type_for_alias`, which has no alias for `timestamp[us, tz=Europe/Brussels]`. Simply allowing the write produces parquet that fails to read back:  ``` ValueError: No type alias for timestamp[us, tz=europe/brussels] ```  So a fix needs a metadata-format change on the registered `pandas.interval` extension type, which has cross-implementation compatibility implications and seems worth its own discussion.  ### Expected Behavior  `pa.array(ser)` succeeds for a tz-aware interval subtype, and the result round-trips through parquet back to the same `IntervalDtype`.

body: # pandas `read_pickle` RCE via Ungated `pickle.load` on the Documented Persistence Format  ## Affected Component  - **Package:** `pandas` (pandas-dev); **Module:** `pandas/io/pickle.py` - **Public API:** `pandas.read_pickle(filepath_or_buffer, compression='infer', storage_options=None)` — entry `io/pickle.py:131`, sink at `:233`  ## Affected Versions  - Dynamic verification on pandas 2.2.3 and 2.3.3 (Python 3.10; 3.0.5's wheel requires py≥3.11 — source-verified instead): `io/pickle.py` carries the identical bare `pickle.load` at `:233` (3.0.5). title: ENH: Allow assign() lambdas to optionally receive the target column as a second argument
body: ### Feature Type  - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas  - [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas  - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  Using the ```df.assign(col_name=lambda df: df[col_name])```method is specially helpful when a user wants to modify and perform operations on multiple columns at once, it provides high readability for these scenarios. body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  ```python  from io import StringIO  import pandas as pd  csv = """id,A,B,C 1,1.5,x,1 2,,x,2 3,2.0,x,3 """  df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(csv), dtype={"A": "double[pyarrow]"}, keep_default_na=False) df = df[["A", "B", "C"]] df["A"] = df["A"].fillna(0) print(df) print("isna:", pd.isna(df["A"]).tolist()) ```  ### Issue Description  Bug in Arrow float conversion: empty strings become IEEE NaN, so fillna does not fill them  When converting string data (e.g. CSV empty fields ,,) to a floating PyArrow dtype, empty strings are not NA (pd.isna("") is False). to_numeric turns them into IEEE NaN, and _from_sequence_of_strings builds pa.array(..., mask=isna(strings)) with that mask all-False. The NaN is stored as a value (null_count=0), not a pyarrow null.  Default pandas 3 semantics treat NaN as NA (is_nan_na() is True), but isna / fillna only look at is_null(). Result: fillna(0) is a no-op.  ### Expected Behavior  Empty CSV fields converted to double[pyarrow] should be pyarrow null (<NA>). isna() is True for those rows, and fillna(0) replaces them with 0.0.  ### Installed Versions  <details>  >>> pd.show_versions()  INSTALLED VERSIONS ------------------ commit                : e68db09ecf6427d1b62e565bacf17f2e525a3032 python                : 3.13.5 python-bits           : 64 OS                    : Windows OS-release            : 11 Version               : 10.0.26200 machine               : AMD64 processor             : Intel64 Family 6 Model 151 Stepping 5, GenuineIntel byteorder             : little LC_ALL                : None LANG                  : en_

title: ENH: Disclose offending values in `IntervalArray._validate`
body: ### Feature Type  - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas  - [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas  - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  When using `IntervalIndex.from_breaks` one ends up at `IntervalArray._validate` which, among others asserts that the left end of the interval is `<=` to the right end.  Yet, it does not disclose the offending values and just raises a generic `left side of interval must be <= right side` `ValueError`. The provided values for the `IntervalArray` may be long so the user may not be able to easily spot the offenders.  ### Feature Description  At this point an `Exception` is raised so one can assume the the library has completed its task. Hence a slight overhead for a improved error message may be acceptable. Only challenge is to not overcharge the error message, in case there are many offenders.  One possible solution could be to change  ```python         if not (left[left_mask] <= right[left_mask]).all():             msg = "left side of interval must be <= right side" ```  to something like (pseudo code)  ```python order_offenders = left[left_mask] > right[left_mask] if order_offenders.any():     msg = f"left side of interval must be <= right side. offending intervals: {zip(left[order_offenders], right[order_offenders]}" ```  ### Alternative Solutions  Alternatively, if this seems to risky or resource intensive, maybe just printing the first 5 offending indices is already helpful  (pseudocode)  ```python order_offenders = left[left_mask] > right[left_mask] if order_offenders.any():     msg = f"left side of interval must be <= right side. offending locations: {order_offenders[order_offenders].index.head(5)}" ```  ### Additional Context  _No response_

body: ### Feature Type  - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas  - [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas  - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  Oftentimes data is stored in plain text files. title: DISCUSSION:  Should `pandas` allow any non-string iterable for various arguments?
body: Discussed in Dev Meeting 8/12/26.  Inspired by https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas-stubs/issues/1876  For various methods/constructors in `pandas`, we indicate that the arguments should be "array-like".  This includes `list`, `Sequence` (but not strings), numpy arrays.  In some cases at runtime, we also allow other iterables (e.g., dicts, generators), and disallow some iterables (e.g., sets), although this is not completely documented.  Examples: ```python  pd.Series(set([1,2,3]))  # Rejected at runtime pd.Index(set([1,2,3]))  # Accepted at runtime pd.Series("abc")  # Accepted at runtime, but treated as scalar - produces Series of length 1 pd.Series({"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3})  # Produces series with dict keys as index, dict values as values pd.Index({"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3}) # Uses keys as the values of the index def square_generator(limit):     num = 0     while num < limit:         yield num ** 2         num += 1    pd.Index(square_generator(5))  # Accepted at runtime ```  The API is inconsistent, as is the documentation.  There are 2 possible ways we can handle this in pandas.  1. Be more restrictive as to what is allowed in the API - it should be an "ordered sequence" (but not a string), possibly not a generator.  Implement these restrictions in the code, support them in `pandas-stubs`, with the idea that users will know if they are writing valid code before runtime. 2. Allow any iterable (including sets, but not strings), which might have unpredictable behavior at runtime, but produces a cleaner API.  We would like to hear the opinions of the community on this, and are open to alternative solutions.  @pandas-dev/pandas-core @pandas-dev/pandas-stubs-team @pandas-dev/pandas-triage

Current code: ``` s = pd.Series(["a", "b", "c", "a"], dtype="category") s new_categories = ["Group %s" % g for g in s.cat.categories] s = s.cat.rename_categories(new_categories) s # You can also pass a dict-like object to map the renaming s = s.cat.rename_categories({1: "x", 2: "y", 3: "z"}) s ``` By the time the dict-rename line runs, s's categories are already ["Group a", "Group b", "Group c"] (strings), not 1/2/3. GH-66510 / GH-66520 closed this for parsing and construction. title: BUG: datetimelike arithmetic landing on the NaT sentinel returns NaT, plus float64 precision loss in timedelta64 arithmetic/reductions
body: Follow-up to GH-66510 / GH-66520, which fixed the *parsing and construction* half of the "value lands on the `NaT` sentinel" problem (`parsers.pyx`, `conversion.pyx`, `strptime.pyx`, `Timestamp.replace`). The *arithmetic* half is still open, and while investigating it I found an adjacent family of `float64` precision bugs in `timedelta64` arithmetic and reductions.  All reproducers below are against `082e77392bd` (main as of 2026-07-29).  Two distinct root causes, filed together because they were found together and overlap in the code they touch — happy to split into separate issues if that's easier to triage.  ---  ## 1. `NPY_NAT` is `int64.min`, so arithmetic landing on it silently becomes `NaT`  A computed value equal to `NPY_NAT` is perfectly representable in `int64`, but is indistinguishable from `NaT` once stored. Today it is silently read back as `NaT` rather than raising. This affects scalars and arrays across all four datetimelike types.  The scalar and vectorized paths also disagree about *which* error to raise one step further out, so you can't paper over it with a `try/except`.  ```python import pandas as pd from pandas import Timedelta, Timestamp from pandas.core.dtypes.dtypes import PeriodDtype  # one ns past the bound -> NaT; two ns past -> raises Timedelta.min - Timedelta(1, "ns")                  # NaT          <- should raise Timedelta.min - Timedelta(2, "ns")                  # OverflowError  pd.array([Timedelta.min]) - Timedelta(1, "ns")      # <TimedeltaArray> [NaT]   <- should raise  Timestamp.min.as_unit("ns") - Timedelta(1, "ns")    # NaT          <- should raise pd.to_datetime([Timestamp.min]).as_unit("ns") - Timedelta(1, "ns")                                                     # DatetimeIndex(['NaT'])   <- should raise  per = pd.Period._from_ordinal(-(2**63) + 1, PeriodDtype("ns")) per - 1                                             # NaT          <- should raise pd.PeriodIndex([per]) - 1                           # PeriodIndex(['NaT'])

body: Follow-ups found while fixing GH-66510 for the vectorized offset paths. Each is pre-existing on `main` (verified at `082e7739`) and out of scope for that PR, but they are the same family of bug: arithmetic on the raw int64 datetime64 values either lands on the `NaT` sentinel or leaves the representable range without being reported as such. Two separate off-by-a-dimension mistakes combine to cause it:  1. `ExponentialMovingWindow.online` builds the deltas array from the **column** count    rather than the row count:     ```python    # pandas/core/window/ewm.py    update_deltas = np.ones(        max(self._selected_obj.shape[-1] - 1, 0), dtype=np.float64    )    ```  2. `online_ewma` then indexes that array with the **column** index `j`, taken from    `numba.prange(len(cur))`, rather than the row index `i` — despite the comment    immediately above it stating the intended contract:     ```python    # pandas/core/window/online.py    for j in numba.prange(len(cur)):        ...        # note that len(deltas) = len(vals) - 1 and deltas[i] is to be        # used in conjunction with vals[i+1]        old_wt[j] *= old_wt_factor ** deltas[j - 1]    ```  For a 1-column frame, (1) makes `update_deltas` a length-0 array, so `deltas[j - 1]` with `j = 0` is an out-of-bounds read on an empty array. Under numba's default (bounds checking off) this yields `0.0`, so `old_wt_factor ** 0 == 1` and `old_wt` never decays.  This is why it has gone unnoticed: for a `Series` and for frames with **2 or more** columns, every in-range index and the wrapped `-1` index all happen to hold

Replacing the nanosecond field with `192` names the wall time one nanosecond earlier, whose int64 representation is exactly `iNaT` (`-2**63`).  `npy_datetimestruct_to_datetime` returns that value without raising, and `replace` does not check for it, so we construct a `Timestamp` whose `_value` is the NaT sentinel but which is not `NaT`. It reprs as a normal timestamp, `pd.isna` reports `False`, and it compares equal to itself — the corruption only surfaces once the value reaches array-land, where it is reinterpreted as `NaT`:  ```python pd.Series([ts]).iloc[0]          # NaT pd.DatetimeIndex([ts])[0]        # NaT ```  It is a single-value hole. title: BUG: unexercised divmod/rdivmod in tests / always False assertion
body: Hello. Wasn't really using `pandas` - I was testing something inside `ruff`, but I've stumbled upon the following test in pandas codebase:  https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/3ea5174d8f7280be22a41b7f4d45ed32db9bc07b/pandas/tests/scalar/test_na_scalar.py#L65-L66  Note that it's using `op(NA, other) is (NA, NA)` - `(NA, NA)` will result in a fresh tuple object on each run, so there's no way `op(NA, other)` had the same object, so effectively this assertion is always false.   I don't fully understand the semantics of the test, but the typical fix for this to use `==` -  `op(NA, other) == (NA, NA)`, instead of relying on `is`.  Generic Python example:	 ```python >>> a = object() >>> (a, a) is (a, a) False >>> (a, a) is (a, a) False >>> (a, a) is (a, a) False >>> (a, a) == (a, a) True >>> (a, a) == (a, a) True >>> (a, a) == (a, a) True ```  Example with pandas: ```python >>> from pandas._libs.missing import NA >>> result = divmod(NA, 3) >>> result (<NA>, <NA>) >>> result is (NA, NA) False >>> result == (NA, NA) True ```  But in theory CI should have flagged it, if it would be just always-false assertion and the code above was introduced a while ago - https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/commit/48368ad6f9087e2e4e4c5236d5492a412ce9d826, so there's another part to this story.  This test is using `all_arithmetic_functions` fixture: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/3ea5174d8f7280be22a41b7f4d45ed32db9bc07b/pandas/conftest.py#L1097-L1115  Looking at the list of params, divmod / rdivmod doesn't seem to be ever exercised, therefore this error never surfaced. So this branch is a dead code and to avoid slipping errors needs a coverage that can be provided by adding `divmod` and `rdivmo` to the fixture parameters.

title: API: read_sas should decode text by default instead of returning bytes
body: ### Feature Type  - [X] Changing existing functionality in pandas  ### Problem Description  `read_sas` defaults to `encoding=None`, which returns character columns as object-dtype `bytes`:  ```python >>> pd.read_sas("test1.sas7bdat")["Column2"] 0    b'pear' dtype: object ```  sas7bdat files record their encoding in the header, so pandas can usually decode without being told. It is also now the only pandas reader that returns bytes by default.  ### Feature Description  Deprecate the current default and change it to `encoding="infer"`, which decodes using the header-declared encoding (falling back to `latin-1` when the code is unrecognized). For XPORT, which has no encoding field, `"infer"` means `ISO-8859-1` — matching `XportReader`'s own default, which `read_sas` currently overrides with `None`.  `encoding=None` stays available for users who want raw bytes.  ### Alternative Solutions  Leave the default and require every user to pass `encoding=`.

body: ### Feature Type  - [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas  - [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas  - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  I wish read_csv's UnicodeDecodeError gave me a hint about what to try next, instead of just failing with no direction.  When read_csv hits a UnicodeDecodeError (e.g. a Windows Excel export saved as cp1252), the error gives no indication that trying a different encoding is the likely fix.  Reproducible example (pandas 3.0.2):  with open('test.csv', 'wb') as f:     f.write(b'name,note\n')     f.write(b'test,em' + bytes([0x97]) + b'dash\n')  # valid cp1252, invalid utf-8  import pandas as pd pd.read_csv('test.csv')  Result: UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0x97 in position 17: invalid start byte  This is a very common situation, Windows Excel commonly exports CSVs as cp1252, not utf-8, and the fix is almost always trying encoding='latin-1' or encoding='cp1252'. But nothing in the error message points there, so new users often don't realize encoding is even the problem.  ### Feature Description  Append a short hint to the UnicodeDecodeError raised during CSV parsing when the default utf-8 encoding fails and the user hasn't explicitly set encoding. body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  ```python import pandas as pd import datetime  ts = pd.Series(     [pd.Timestamp("2024-01-01"), None, pd.Timestamp("2024-06-15")],     dtype="timestamp[ns][pyarrow]", )  # Cross-type comparison: timestamp vs datetime.date result_eq = ts == datetime.date(2024, 1, 1) print(result_eq) # 0    False   ← should be True (values are equal) # 1    False   ← should be <NA> (null propagation) # 2    False # dtype: bool[pyarrow]  # Same-type comparison works correctly result_same = ts == pd.Timestamp("2024-01-01") print(result_same) # 0     True # 1     <NA> # 2    False # dtype: bool[pyarrow] ```  ### Issue Description  When comparing a Series with ArrowDtype timestamp type against a `datetime.date` scalar (or `date32[day][pyarrow]` Series), pandas falls back to object-level comparison instead of delegating to pyarrow's `pc.equal()`. title: ENH: Support `tz_convert` on naive timestamps when naive tz specified
body: ### Feature Type  - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas  - [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas  - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  It is quite common to defensively convert-or-assume timestamps to UTC, which means writing something like this:  ```python def my_function(df: pd.Dataframe, time: pd.Timestamp) -> pd.Dataframe:     if time.tzinfo is None:         time = time.tz_localize("UTC")     else:         time = time.tz_convert("UTC")     ...     return df.assign(time=time) ```  Alternatively an inline if can be used  ```python time = time.tz_localize("UTC") if time.tz is None else time.tz_convert("UTC") ```  But this is slightly longwinded, so often helper functions are repeated in loads of modules  ```python def _ensure_utc(time: pd.Timestamp) -> pd.Timestamp:     return (         time.tz_localize("UTC")         if time.tz is None         else time.tz_convert("UTC")     ) ```  My opinion is that neither the rather long if..else expression nor the usually-not-consistently-named helper method are very readable. There can also be challenges around proper typing on the helper method, when support for e.g. series and datetime index is required as well. This feature request is essentially asking for a shorthand that is native to Pandas for this pattern.  ### Feature Description  Add a keyword argument to `tz_convert` which specifies how naive timestamps should be interpreted, instead of raising an error:   ```python time = time.tz_convert("UTC", naive_tz="UTC") ```  It would be functionally equivalent to `time.tz_localize("UTC") if time.tz is None else time.tz_convert("UTC")` - just a shorthand. title: BUG: read_csv(dtype="category") ignores dtype_backend for the c and python engines
body:
### Reproducible Example  ```python import pandas as pd from io import StringIO  data = "a,b
1,2
3,4
"  df = pd.read_csv(     StringIO(data), dtype={"a": "category"}, dtype_backend="numpy_nullable" ) df.dtypes # a    category # b       Int64  df["a"].cat.categories.dtype # dtype('int64')   <- numpy, but `b` in the same frame is Int64 ```  ### Issue Description  Since GH-56044, `read_csv` with `dtype="category"` infers numeric and boolean categories instead of leaving them as strings. That inference does not consult `dtype_backend`, so the c and python engines produce numpy-dtyped categories even when every other column in the same frame gets a nullable or arrow dtype.  Category element dtype for `"a
1
2"`, against what the same column gets *without* `dtype="category"`:  | engine | `numpy_nullable` | `pyarrow` | |---|---|---| | c | `int64` (non-cat: `Int64`) | `int64` (non-cat: `int64[pyarrow]`) | | python | `int64` (non-cat: `Int64`) | `int64[pyarrow]` :heavy_check_mark: | | pyarrow | `Int64` :heavy_check_mark: | `int64[pyarrow]` :heavy_check_mark: |  Three of six combinations disagree with the non-categorical result. The current behavior is pinned by `test_categorical_dtype_non_default_dtype_backend`.  Two notes on why the passing cells already work, since they're inconsistent for different reasons:  - The **pyarrow engine** is correct only incidentally: `_post_convert_dtypes` in `pandas/io/_util.py` is gated on `dtype_backend is lib.no_default or dtype_backend == "numpy"`, so an explicit backend skips the `IntegerDtype`->numpy downcast that would otherwise apply. - The **python engine + `pyarrow`** case works because its values arrive as arrow-backed strings and `to_numeric` returns `int64[pyarrow]` directly -- not because the backend was consulted. title: PERF: union_indexes is slow for homogeneous RangeIndexes during DataFrame concatenation
body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  ### Problem Description Concatenating many small DataFrames with homogeneous (often identical) columns or index `RangeIndex` objects spends significant time in `union_indexes` and `RangeIndex.union`.   For example, when concatenating 2,000 small DataFrames along `axis=0` with identical columns, `union_indexes` is called on a list of 2,000 `RangeIndex(0, 10)` objects. Currently, this performs a loop of 1,999 sequential `result.union(other)` calls, which incurs high type check, name reconciliation (`_get_reconciled_name_object`), and new index object creation overhead (consuming over 50% of the runtime).  ### Reproducible Example ```python import pandas as pd import time  # 2,000 small DataFrames with identical columns dfs = [pd.DataFrame(0, index=[i], columns=pd.RangeIndex(0, 10)) for i in range(2000)]  t0 = time.perf_counter() pd.concat(dfs) t1 = time.perf_counter() print(f"Concatenation time: {t1 - t0:.4f} seconds") ```  ### Proposed Solution Add a fast-path inside `union_indexes` when all input indices are `RangeIndex` instances:  - Deduplicate them quickly using a set of (range, name) tuples. - If all unique non-empty indices share the same step and name, check if they are contiguous/overlapping (no gaps). - If they are contiguous, directly return a single `RangeIndex` spanning the start/stop range. - Otherwise, fall back to the standard union logic but only iterate over the deduplicated unique `RangeIndexes`.   ### Prior Performance  _No response_

title: BUG: merge_asof says "tolerance must be positive" but accepts tolerance=0
body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.  ### Reproducible Example  ```python import pandas as pd  left = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 5, 10], "left_val": ["a", "b", "c"]}) right = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 6, 10], "right_val": ["A", "B", "C"]})  # tolerance=0 is accepted and meaningful: exact-match-only print(pd.merge_asof(left, right, on="a", tolerance=0)) #     a left_val right_val # 0   1        a         A # 1   5        b       NaN   <- no exact match within 0 # 2  10        c         C  # but a negative tolerance is rejected with a message that claims 0 is invalid too: pd.merge_asof(left, right, on="a", tolerance=-1) # MergeError: tolerance must be positive ```  ### Issue Description  `merge_asof` accepts `tolerance=0` (which means exact-match-only, a meaningful asof semantic), but the error raised for an invalid `tolerance` says it `must be positive`. The three guards in `_MergeOperation`/`_AsOfMerge` reject only strictly-negative values:  ```python if self.tolerance < Timedelta(0):     raise MergeError("tolerance must be positive") ... if self.tolerance < 0:     raise MergeError("tolerance must be positive") ```  So `0` is accepted, yet "must be positive" (which means `> 0`) excludes it. The message is inconsistent with the guard.  ### Expected Behavior  The message should say `tolerance must be non-negative`, matching the values the guard actually accepts.  ### Installed Versions  <details>  Reproduced on `main` and pandas 3.0.3.  </details>

body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.  ### Reproducible Example  ```python import pandas as pd  mi = pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples([("a", 1), ("b", 2)], names=["l", "n"]) mi.set_levels([["x", "y"]], level=0) ```  ### Issue Description  `MultiIndex.set_levels` (and `set_codes`) raise a self-contradictory message when a **single, scalar** `level` is paired with a **nested** (list-of-lists) value:  ``` TypeError: Levels must be list-like ```  The value `[["x", "y"]]` *is* list-like — that's precisely why control reaches this branch. In `_require_listlike` (`pandas/core/indexes/multi.py`), the scalar-level branch first rejects a non-list-like `arr` with `"must be list-like"`, and then rejects a *nested* `arr` (a list of lists) with the **same** string, which is a copy-paste of the first message:  ```python if level is not None and not is_list_like(level):     if not is_list_like(arr):         raise TypeError(f"{arrname} must be list-like")          # arr is not list-like — message correct     if len(arr) > 0 and is_list_like(arr[0]):         raise TypeError(f"{arrname} must be list-like")          # arr IS list-like (nested) — message wrong ```  For a scalar level the value must be a *flat* list-like, so the second message should say that, not repeat "must be list-like".  ### Expected Behavior  The nested-value case should raise a message that names the real constraint, e.g.:  ``` TypeError: Levels must be list-like, not a list of lists-like ```  which mirrors the existing `"must be list of lists-like"` message used for the list-valued `level` branch.  ### Installed Versions  <details>  main branch (`_require_listlike` in `pandas/core/indexes/multi.py`).  </details>

title: ENH: Optimize Series.apply User-Defined Functions (UDFs) via JIT Compilation Engine Option
body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  ### Problem Description Invoking `.apply()` with custom Python functions is notoriously slow in Pandas because it loops over rows in pure Python (the "UDF bottleneck"). For large Series, this element-by-element interpreter call pattern adds massive overhead.  While Pandas supports Numba engines in GroupBy and Rolling window methods, standard `.apply()` lacks direct JIT compilation engines to accelerate simple mathematical/branching row-level functions.  ### Proposed Feature Introduce a JIT compilation execution engine option inside `Series.apply()`. 1. **Explicit Opt-in**: Support `engine="numba"` and `engine_kwargs` parameters in `Series.apply()`. If specified, JIT compile the UDF using Numba and execute via a fast parallelized JIT loop dispatcher. 2. **Global Configuration Option**: Support automatic transparent JIT execution on large numeric/datetime Series ($\ge 50,000$ elements) if the global option `pd.set_option("compute.use_numba", True)` is enabled. 3. **Correctness & Error Boundaries**:     - When explicitly opted-in (`engine="numba"`), raise a `NumbaUtilError` or `ValueError` if compilation or input dtype constraints fail.    - When implicitly run via the global configuration, fall back silently to the Python interpreter on any compilation warnings/errors to maintain 100% backward-compatibility.  ### Code Example / Benchmark Comparison For a UDF with branching math operations over a Series of 1,000,000 floats: ```python def my_func(x):     if x > 0:         return math.sin(x) * math.exp(-x)     else:         return math.cos(x) * 1.5 ``` ### Standard apply: ~870ms ### JIT apply (engine="numba", cached): ~37ms  (~23.4x speedup)

body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  **Description:**  ### Problem Description Currently, calling `DataFrame.dropna()` on a homogeneous single-block DataFrame (e.g. a float64 or object DataFrame) goes through the general multi-block BlockManager reconciliation and `.loc` index slicing path. This involves: 1. Allocating a temporary boolean DataFrame (`notna_obj`) to check null entries. 2. Allocating a temporary boolean Series (`mask`) during reduction along `axis=1`. 3. Invoking `.loc[mask]`, which checks label alignment and calls `BlockManager.reindex_indexer()`. title: PERF: Skip full array allocation in RangeIndex.isin for small query inputs
body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  **Description:**  ### Problem Description Currently, calling `RangeIndex.isin(values)` delegates to the generic `Index.isin` implementation. This accesses `self._values`, which forces the RangeIndex to fully instantiate its entire integer range array in memory (e.g. allocating a contiguous 80MB NumPy array for a RangeIndex of size 10,000,000), followed by building a hash table or running `algos.isin` on the generated array.  If the search query `values` has only a small number of elements, this is highly inefficient.  ### Proposed Optimization Implement `RangeIndex.isin` directly. When `len(values) < len(self)`, we can allocate a boolean output array of size `len(self)` and mathematically check which query values are in the RangeIndex using CPython's $O(1)$ `range.__contains__` check. If present, we set the corresponding boolean array location in $O(1)$ using the computed index: `idx = (val - start) // step`  For large queries where `len(values) >= len(self)`, we delegate back to `super().isin(values)` to leverage C-level array hashing.  ### Performance Impact - Eliminates the memory allocation of the full RangeIndex integer array (80MB for a 10M range index). - Speeds up membership checks by bypassing array generation and hash searches.   ### Installed Versions  <details>  Replace this line with the output of pd.show_versions()  </details>   ### Prior Performance  _No response_

Cache the `pkg_dir` and `test_dir` paths globally at the module level. 2. title: Add type hints to public API functions
body: ## Feature Request  ### Summary Adding type hints to public API functions would significantly improve developer experience and enable better tooling support.  ### Motivation - IDEs can provide better autocomplete and inline documentation - Static type checkers like `mypy` can catch bugs before runtime - New contributors can understand the expected inputs/outputs faster - Type hints serve as machine-checked documentation  ### Proposed Change Add type annotations to all public functions:  ```python # Before: def process(data, config=None):     ...  # After: from typing import Optional, Dict, Any  def process(data: Dict[str, Any], config: Optional[Dict] = None) -> bool:     ... ```  ### Additional Context This is a non-breaking change and can be done incrementally, starting with the most-used public functions.

No Python traceback is produced.  ### Issue Description  On Python 3.14, `pandas==3.0.4` segfaults when constructing a `Timedelta` if the installed numpy is in the 2.3.x–2.4.x range. The crash is a hard SIGSEGV (exit 139), single-process and fully deterministic.  The numpy `_multiarray_umath` shared object is not stripped, so the faulting frame symbolizes exactly:  ``` #0  PyUFunc_f_f (numpy/_core/_multiarray_umath.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so + 0xd5f58)         => mov (%rdx),%r15            # registers at fault: rdx = 0x6, rcx = 0x0 #1  pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so #2  pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so #3  slot_tp_new -> type_call -> _PyObject_MakeTpCall    # Timedelta(1, unit='D') ```  `PyUFunc_f_f` is numpy's generic float32 unary ufunc inner loop, whose signature is `(char **args, npy_intp *dimensions, npy_intp *steps, void *func)`. At the fault, `rdx` (the `steps` pointer) holds `0x6` and `rcx` (`func`) is `NULL`; the loop dereferences `steps` and segfaults. title: DataFrame constructed from Index or Series mutates the original object
body: # BUG: `DataFrame` constructed from `Index` or `Series` mutates the original object  ## Description  When constructing a `DataFrame` from a pandas `Index` or `Series` containing string data, any modifications made to the new `DataFrame` unexpectedly mutate the original `Index` or `Series`. This occurs even when `.copy()` is explicitly called before passing the object to the constructor — the underlying array is reused rather than being independently tracked.  This bug does **not** affect integer-backed `Index` or `Series` objects, only string (and other extension array) types.  Additionally, this can break internal invariants — displaying a `DataFrame` whose columns were modified this way has been observed to crash the IPython kernel.  ## Reproducible Example  ```python import pandas as pd  # Bug with Index input df = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2], 'B': [3, 4]}) columns = pd.DataFrame(data=df.columns.copy()) columns.loc[0, 0] = 'C' assert df.columns[0] == 'A'  # FAILS — original Index was mutated  # Bug with string Index directly idx = pd.Index(["A", "B"]) df2 = pd.DataFrame(idx) df2.iloc[0, 0] = "C" print(idx)  # Index(['C', 'B'], dtype='str') — original mutated  # Bug with string Series input ser = pd.Series(["A", "B"]) df3 = pd.DataFrame(ser) df3.iloc[0, 0] = "C" print(ser)  # 0    C \n 1    B — original mutated  # No bug with integer Index (works correctly) idx_int = pd.Index([0, 1]) df4 = pd.DataFrame(idx_int) df4.iloc[0, 0] = 100 print(idx_int)  # Index([0, 1], dtype='int64') — unchanged ```  ## Expected Behavior  ```python idx = pd.Index(["A", "B"]) df = pd.DataFrame(idx) df.iloc[0, 0] = "C" print(idx)  # Expected: Index(['A', 'B'], dtype='str') — unchanged ```  ## Actual Behavior  ```python print(idx)  # Actual: Index(['C', 'B'], dtype='str') — original was silently mutated ```  ## Installed Versions  <details>  ``` pandas     : 3.1.0.dev0+37.g98ffe4c45e numpy      : 2.3.5 python     : 3.11.14 OS         : Windows 10 ```  Run `pd.show_versions()` for full detail

title: [BUG] NULL pointer dereference in total_seconds (ujson encoder)
body: ## Bug Description  In `pandas/_libs/src/vendored/ujson/python/objToJSON.c`, the `total_seconds` function calls `PyObject_CallMethod` without NULL check, then uses the unsafe `PyFloat_AS_DOUBLE` macro on the result.  ## Location  `pandas/_libs/src/vendored/ujson/python/objToJSON.c:305-309`  ## Code  ```c static npy_float64 total_seconds(PyObject *td) {   PyObject *value = PyObject_CallMethod(td, "total_seconds", NULL);   const npy_float64 double_val = PyFloat_AS_DOUBLE(value);  // no NULL check, no type check   Py_DECREF(value);   return double_val; } ```  ## Impact  `PyObject_CallMethod` can return NULL on error. `PyFloat_AS_DOUBLE` is an unsafe macro that directly accesses struct fields without any NULL or type check. When `value` is NULL: - `PyFloat_AS_DOUBLE(NULL)` dereferences NULL → immediate segfault - `Py_DECREF(NULL)` also crashes  This is triggered during JSON serialization of timedelta objects when `total_seconds()` raises an exception.  ## Suggested Fix  ```c static npy_float64 total_seconds(PyObject *td) {   PyObject *value = PyObject_CallMethod(td, "total_seconds", NULL);   if (value == NULL) return -1.0;   const npy_float64 double_val = PyFloat_AsDouble(value);  // safe version   Py_DECREF(value);   return double_val; } ```  ## Environment  - pandas version: current main - Affected API: `ujson.dumps()` / `pd.io.json` on timedelta objects

title: [BUG] Use-after-free in int64ToIso: result freed but still dereferenced
body: ## Bug Description  In `pandas/_libs/src/datetime/date_conversions.c`, when `make_iso_8601_datetime` fails, `result` is freed via `PyObject_Free` but the function does NOT return. Execution falls through to `strlen(result)` and `return result`, using a freed pointer.  ## Location  `pandas/_libs/src/datetime/date_conversions.c:59-69`  ## Code  ```c ret_code = make_iso_8601_datetime(&dts, result, *len, 0, base); if (ret_code != 0) {     PyErr_SetString(PyExc_ValueError,                     "Could not convert datetime value to string");     PyObject_Free(result);  // freed here } // falls through — missing return NULL! *len = strlen(result);      // USE AFTER FREE return result;              // returns freed pointer ```  ## Impact  - Use-after-free: `strlen` reads freed memory - The freed pointer is returned to the caller, which will read/use corrupted data - Can cause crashes, incorrect datetime string output, or memory corruption  ## Suggested Fix  Add `return NULL;` after `PyObject_Free(result);`:  ```c if (ret_code != 0) {     PyErr_SetString(PyExc_ValueError,                     "Could not convert datetime value to string");     PyObject_Free(result);     return NULL; } ```  ## Environment  - pandas version: current main - Affected API: datetime-to-ISO-string conversion paths

title: Potential resource leak when exception occurs during file operation

Open a file without using a context manager 2. Raise an exception before closing the file 3. title: ENH: Support %N directive in strptime parsing (to_datetime / Timestamp with format=)
body: ### Feature Type  - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas  ### Problem Description  GH-29461 / PR GH-64899 added a `%N` directive to `Timestamp.strftime` and the array-level `strftime`, formatting nanoseconds as a 9-digit zero-padded number. The parsing side does not accept it, so `%N` output doesn't round-trip with the same format string:  ```python >>> ts = pd.Timestamp("2020-03-14 15:32:52.192548651") >>> fmt = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%N" >>> pd.to_datetime(ts.strftime(fmt), format=fmt) ValueError: 'N' is a bad directive in format '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%N' ```  Note that pandas' strptime already parses nanoseconds via `%f` (it accepts 1-9 digits, an extension over the stdlib's 6), so this is about symmetry and round-tripping rather than new capability. Suggested in https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/64899#pullrequestreview-4481273478.  ### Feature Description  Accept `%N` in `format=` for `to_datetime`, `Timestamp`, and related parsing paths, matching exactly 9 digits (vs `%f`'s 1-9). Likely just an entry next to `"f"` in the `TimeRE` class and corresponding handling in `strptime.pyx`.  ### Alternative Solutions  Keep parsing via `%f`, which already handles 9 digits — but then a format string built for `%N` output can't be reused for parsing.  ### Additional Context  `Period.strftime` has long supported `%n`/`%N` for formatting only; linux `date` uses `%N` for nanoseconds.

title: BUG: to_parquet (pyarrow engine) opens the local file path twice
body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  ```python import builtins import os  import pandas as pd  # Spy on Python-level opens of the destination path. target = "test.parquet" opens = [] real_open = builtins.open  def spy_open(file, *args, **kwargs):     if os.path.abspath(os.fspath(file)) == os.path.abspath(target):         opens.append(args)     return real_open(file, *args, **kwargs)  builtins.open = spy_open try:     pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]}).to_parquet(target, engine="pyarrow") finally:     builtins.open = real_open  print(f"pandas opened the destination {len(opens)} time(s) at the Python level")  # Observed: 1  -> pandas opens the file itself via get_handle... # ...but pyarrow ALSO opens the same path through its C++ layer and does the # actual writing, so the path is opened twice per to_parquet call.  # On Linux this is also visible at the syscall level: # strace -f -e trace=openat python -c \ #  "import pandas as pd; pd.DataFrame({'a':[1]}).to_parquet('x.parquet')" 2>&1 \ #  | grep -c 'x.parquet' # two openat() calls for the same path ```  ### Issue Description  For a local filesystem path, `to_parquet` with the pyarrow engine resolves the path through `pandas.io.common.get_handle` inside `_get_path_or_handle`, then unwraps the handle's .name back to a string and hands that string to pyarrow. pyarrow then opens  the same path a second time through its own (memory-mapped, multithreaded) C++ I/O layer, which is where the read/write actually happens. So every local-path call opens the destination/source twice.  Consequences: - On POSIX: a wasted `open()`/`close()` syscall

title: API: how to handle time zone (DST) transitions in the distant future?
body: Historically, by using `pytz` by default for time zones, tz-aware data had wrong offsets for DST periods after 2038 (e.g. see https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/33061 and https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/28207, and documented at https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/version/3.0/user_guide/timeseries.html#working-with-time-zones (scroll down to the 5th(!) warning box), sidenote: we should update this).  The same happens if you were using `dateutil.tz` time zones, and the short summary is that pytz and dateutil are only parsing the Version 1 TZif files, those don't include a "rule" for future times, and therefore typically include transitions times extrapolated to the future, but because of 32bit are limited to dates up to 2038.  This issue was fixed by switching to `zoneinfo` by default (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/34916) in pandas 3.0, since zoneinfo supports the newer versions of TZif files, and can use a rule-based logic for determining the offset for distant dates.  However, then after improving the performance for `zoneinfo` timezones to also use our internal fast binary search of the transition points (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/64379) in pandas 3.0.3, this changed this behaviour again, because now we have to pre-populate our array of transition dates (to use for the binary search), and the linked PR decided to do that up to 2100 (meaning we only get correct offsets up to 2100, and not for later dates, see the example below).   In https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/65705, I am extending that cut-off from 2100 to 2262.  While having tz-aware data so far in the future is a bit a debatable use case, having an arbitrary cut off after which it behaves differently is not ideal. title: ENH/API: Architectural Audit - Are other inplace=True methods bypassing CoW reference tracking?
body: ### Feature Type  - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas  - [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas  - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  ### Background While investigating a memory corruption issue yesterday (reported in #65664  and patched in PR #65675 ), I found a structural vulnerability in how the computation engine interacts with Pandas 3.0's Copy-on-Write (CoW) architecture.   Specifically, `df.eval("new=old", inplace=True)` was bypassing CoW protections. The `eval` engine reached into the `BlockManager`, extracted the raw data arrays, evaluated them, and handed them back. Because the data took a detour through the external computation engine, the CoW reference tracking metadata was stripped. The DataFrame assumed the returned array was unshared memory, leading to silent memory corruption when the alias was later modified.  ### The Architectural Question My patch forces an explicit `.copy()` before assignment if `inplace=True` inside `pandas.core.computation.eval`. However, this raises a much larger architectural question: **Are there other C-engine, Cython, or NumExpr-routed methods that are secretly leaking CoW tracking data when `inplace=True` is invoked?**  ### Proposed Audit Targets We know that standard `__setitem__` handles CoW perfectly. But any method that extracts raw arrays, computes externally, and attempts to write back `inplace` is at risk. I propose a systematic audit of the following `inplace=True` methods to ensure they aren't making the same tracking error:  1. **`DataFrame.query(inplace=True)`:** Since this relies on the exact same underlying `pandas.core.computation` engines (`numexpr` / `python`) as `eval`, it is the most likely candidate for a parallel vulnerability. 2. **`DataFrame.where()` & `DataFrame.mask()`:** When backed by external engines or fast-path Cython blocks. 3. **`DataFrame.fillna()` & `DataFrame.replace()`:** Specifically when operating on mixed dtypes that might force a bloc

title: PERF: pandas.io.sql.has_table slow for ADBC driver with large database
body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  We actually noticed the slowness from `pandas.read_sql`, but narrowed the problem down to its call to `has_table`. We're calling `read_sql` with a query so it will always be a miss for `has_table`.  ```python import time import pandas.io.sql as pd_sql from adbc_driver_snowflake.dbapi import connect  with connect("<database URI>") as conn:  # Connection to a large database     start = time.perf_counter()     pd_sql.has_table("foo", conn)  # Where foo does not match a table     end = time.perf_counter()     print(f"Took {end - start} seconds") ```  The problem sees to be in [`pandas.io.sql.ADBCDatabase.has_table`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/io/sql.py#L2429-L2431), which calls [`self.con.adbc_get_objects()`](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/current/python/api/adbc_driver_manager.html#adbc_driver_manager.dbapi.Connection.adbc_get_objects) without passing `depth=`. The default depth is `"all"`, which enumerates objects down to the columns. Adding `depth="tables"` speeds things up dramatically for us—from 53 seconds without `depth="tables"` down to 3 seconds with.  ### Installed Versions  <details>  INSTALLED VERSIONS ------------------ commit                : 9c8bc3e55188c8aff37207a74f1dd144980b8874 python                : 3.12.12 python-bits           : 64 OS                    : Darwin OS-release            : 25.4.0 Version               : Darwin Kernel Version 25.4.0: Thu Mar 19 19:30:44 PDT 2026; root:xnu-12377.101.15~1/RELEASE_ARM64_T6000 machine               : arm64 processor             : arm byteorder             : little LC_ALL                : None LANG                  : en_US.UTF-8 LOCALE                : en_US

body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  ```python import pandas as pd  df = pd.DataFrame(     {'a': range(3), 'b': range(10, 13), 'c': range(3)} ).rename(columns={'b': 'a'})  print(df) print(df.eval('a == 1')) print(pd.eval('a == 1', resolvers=(df,))) ```  ### Issue Description  `Dataframe.eval ` behaves differently from `pandas.eval()` when a `DataFrame` contains duplicated column names. title: BUG: Conversion from np.ma.masked_array to pd.array does not preserve missing values

title: API: tracker for single-element listlike RHS inconsistency in setitem
body: `obj[key] = [42]` (or `np.array([42])`) does different things depending on the accessor, the key shape, the dtype, and the block structure of unrelated columns:  ```python df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [10, 20, 30], "y": [40, 50, 60]},                   index=["a", "b", "c"]).astype(object)  # list RHS df.loc["a", "x"]      = [42]            # cell stores [42] df.loc["a", ["x"]]    = [42]            # cell stores 42 df.loc[["a"], ["x"]]  = [42]            # cell stores 42 df.iloc[0, 0]         = [42]            # cell stores [42] df.iloc[0, [0]]       = [42]            # cell stores 42 df.at["a", "x"]       = [42]            # cell stores [42]  # np.array RHS — yet another set of outcomes df.loc["a", "x"]      = np.array([42])  # cell stores array(42)   (0-D!) df.loc["a", ["x"]]    = np.array([42])  # cell stores np.int64(42) df.loc[["a"], ["x"]]  = np.array([42])  # cell stores 42 df.iloc[0, 0]         = np.array([42])  # cell stores array(42) df.iloc[0, [0]]       = np.array([42])  # cell stores np.int64(42) df.at["a", "x"]       = np.array([42])  # cell stores array(42) ```  Six open issues describe pieces of this directly. Filing as a single umbrella so they can be considered together.  ## Bull's-eye open issues  **#16864 (2017) — One item lists are assigned into dataframes as single items.** `df.loc[[0,1], 'new_col'] = [['one_item'], ['one_item']]` stores `'one_item'` (the inner string) in each row instead of `['one_item']` (the list). The reporter wanted to populate a list-valued column row-by-row and was surprised that single-element nested lists got unwrapped while multi-element ones didn't.  **#25806 (2019) — Effect of assigning list to DataFrame cell depends on unrelated column's type.** `df.loc['a', 'foo'] = ['123']` stores `['123']` on a fresh DataFrame, but the *same* assignment on the same DataFrame stores `'123'` once an unrelated column has been cast to float. Behavior depends on the block layout, not on user intent. Same example shows `.at` and `.loc` div

title: BUG: Index.get_indexer matches pd.NA against NaN for list input but not ndarray input
body: `Index.get_indexer` gives different answers for `[pd.NA]` (list) vs `np.array([pd.NA], dtype=object)` on a NaN-containing index. The list path normalizes `pd.NA` to NaN; the ndarray path doesn't. `Index.get_loc` (scalar lookup) also matches. This propagates into `Index.drop`, which routes through `com.index_labels_to_array` (producing an ndarray) and so cannot drop a NaN-labeled entry given `pd.NA`.  ```python import numpy as np import pandas as pd  idx = pd.Index([np.nan, "b"])  idx.get_loc(np.nan)                              # 0 idx.get_loc(pd.NA)                               # 0  <- matches  idx.get_indexer([pd.NA])                         # array([0])   <- matches idx.get_indexer(np.array([pd.NA], dtype=object)) # array([-1])  <- doesn't idx.get_indexer(pd.Index([pd.NA]))               # array([-1])  <- doesn't  idx.drop([pd.NA])   # KeyError: '[<NA>] not found in axis' idx.drop([np.nan])  # works ```  Surfaces from `merge`: a DataFrame built with `{pd.NA: ...}` has columns coerced to a NaN label, so `merge(left_on=pd.NA, right_on=pd.NA)` resolves keys correctly via `_get_label_or_level_values` (which uses `get_loc`) but fails on the `right_drop` path via `_drop_labels_or_levels` -> `Index.drop`.  The scalar-lookup paths (`get_loc`, list `get_indexer`) treat `pd.NA` as matching NaN; the array-lookup paths (ndarray/Index `get_indexer`, `Index.drop`) don't. Either both should match, or neither should.

title: PERF: skip redundant Index.equals calls in pd.concat
body: ### Problem  `pd.concat` compares the same logical pair of indexes twice:  1. `union_indexes` → `all_indexes_same` (`indexes/api.py:337`) walks the inputs pairwise (`first.equals(idx)` for each other), and returns `indexes[0]` when they all match. 2. Then `_get_result` (`reshape/concat.py:652`) re-runs `new_labels.equals(obj_labels)` per obj to decide whether reindexing is needed — re-asking the same question.  In the common case where input frames are separately-constructed with content-equal-but-identity-distinct column indexes, ~50% of all `Index.equals` calls under `pd.concat` are this duplicate.  ### Numbers (per call, inputs pre-built outside the timer)  | workload | before | after | speedup | |---|---|---|---| | 100 frames, 50 cols, single-block float | 0.62 ms | 0.50 ms | **1.25x** | | 1000 frames, 50 cols, single-block float | 6.76 ms | 5.70 ms | 1.19x | | 100 frames, 20 cols, multi-block (dict-built) | 0.64 ms | 0.49 ms | **1.31x** | | 20 sibling-tables, axis=1, 1000 rows | 0.19 ms | 0.15 ms | 1.25x | | 200 frames built fresh + concat (read-many-files) | 7.96 ms | 7.58 ms | 1.05x |  "After" estimated by short-circuiting duplicate `(id(self), id(other))` pairs with a per-concat memoization cache.  ### Beneficiary  Patterns that build frames separately then concat them: `pd.concat([pd.read_csv(f) for f in files])` and equivalents.  `groupby.apply` and `pd.concat([df.iloc[a:b] for ...])` see **zero** `Index.equals` calls (slices share the parent's Index identity, `_get_distinct_objs` collapses them) — this change is a no-op for those.  ### Proposed change  Return an `all_equal` flag from `union_indexes` when it takes the `all_indexes_same`-True branch, and thread it through `_get_combined_index` → `new_axes` → `_get_result`. When True, `_get_result` skips the per-obj `equals` and uses empty indexers.  Happy to put up a PR.

title: PERF: cache BlockManager.get_dtypes() result
body: ### Problem  `BaseBlockManager.get_dtypes()` (`pandas/core/internals/managers.py:339`) rebuilds an object array on every call:  ```python def get_dtypes(self) -> npt.NDArray[np.object_]:     dtypes = np.array([blk.dtype for blk in self.blocks], dtype=object)     return dtypes.take(self.blknos) ```  It's called from a number of hot paths — `df.dtypes`, `DataFrame.fillna` (`generic.py:6391`), `select_dtypes`/`_get_numeric_data`, `DataFrame.apply` (`frame.py:15751`), `unique_dtypes` in repr/info (`generic.py:7136`), and twice per `iloc` setitem (`indexing.py:944, 975`). For wide, fragmented managers each call is O(nblocks) Python iteration plus an object-array allocation.  ### Numbers (1000-col DataFrame, 335 blocks, mixed f8/i8/object)  | call | current | with cache | speedup | |---|---|---|---| | `mgr.get_dtypes()` | 47 us | 0.08 us | **608x** | | `df.dtypes` | 58 us | 8.7 us | **6.7x** |  Caching saves the full cost on cache hits; `df.dtypes` retains ~8 us of unavoidable Series-construction overhead.  ### Proposed change  Add a `_dtypes_cache` attribute on the manager, populated lazily in `get_dtypes()` and invalidated alongside the existing `_blknos` / `_interleaved_dtype` cache hooks (`managers.py:1411, 1497` and other block-mutation sites). The same invalidation pattern is already in place — adding one more entry is mechanical.  ### Caveats  - The cached array must not be mutated in place by callers. A quick audit of callers shows they only read it (equality checks, `.take`, iteration) — no in-place writes — but worth confirming during review. - `SingleBlockManager` already has only one block; the cache is still cheap and consistent.  Happy to put up a PR.

title: PERF: Replace dateutil-based parser fallback with a regex-based parser in tslibs.parsing

title: PERF: skip to_datetime cache=True overhead for input shapes where it cannot help
body: #### Summary  `to_datetime(..., cache=True)` (the default) unconditionally runs the `_maybe_cache` machinery — `Series(dtype=object)` construction + `should_cache` which iterates up to 500 elements of the input — even on inputs where `_convert_listlike_datetimes` is going to dispatch to a non-parsing path or a path where caching has been measured to never help. On these inputs `cache=True` is strictly slower than `cache=False`, by margins ranging from a few percent to **~520×** at the worst. body: ### Feature Type  - [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas  - [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas  - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  When creating a contingency table using pd.crosstab, if a user specifies normalize='index' while also requesting margins=True, the resulting DataFrame includes the marginal row (at the bottom) but excludes the marginal column (on the right). While the marginal column would mathematically consist of constants (1.0), its omission prevents the generation of a complete "framed" table for reporting and visualization purposes. title: API: Index.take discards fill_value and raises unnecessarily
body: `Index.take` has two bugs when `allow_fill=True` and `fill_value` is passed explicitly:  ### 1. `fill_value` is silently discarded  The caller's `fill_value` is ignored; `self._na_value` is always substituted:  ```python # Note: we discard fill_value and use self._na_value, only relevant #  in the case where allow_fill is True and fill_value is not None taken = algos.take(     values, indices, allow_fill=allow_fill, fill_value=self._na_value ) ```  ### 2. `_can_hold_na` gate raises on integer dtypes  ```python >>> pd.Index([1, 2, 3]).take([0, -1], allow_fill=True, fill_value=99) ValueError: Unable to fill values because Index cannot contain NA ```  The caller provided a valid fill value that the dtype can hold, but `Index.take` rejects it because `_can_hold_na` is False for integer dtypes.  ### Consequences  These force internal callers to bypass `Index.take` and work on the underlying arrays directly:  - **`frame.py` idxmin/idxmax**: `algorithms.take(index._values, ...)` instead of `index.take(...)` - **`reshape/merge.py`**: appends a sentinel value to the index, with a comment: *"We do not use allow_fill and fill_value because it throws a ValueError on integer indices"* - **`indexes/base.py` reset_index**: take-then-putmask as two operations - **`io/formats/excel.py`**: guards `allow_fill` on `levels._can_hold_na` - **`indexes/multi.py`**: `algos.take_nd(lev._values, ...)` instead of `lev.take(...)`  ### Proposed fix  - Respect the caller's `fill_value` - Remove the `_can_hold_na` gate (let the underlying array handle type promotion) - Simplify the workaround sites  This is backward-compatible: the existing gate (`allow_fill=True` + `fill_value is None` → numpy-style take) is preserved, so bare `idx.take(indices)` is unchanged.
