title: BUG: partition_quality raises ZeroDivisionError on graphs with no edges or fewer than two nodes
body: ## Summary  `partition_quality` raises an uncaught `ZeroDivisionError` on graphs with no edges or fewer than two nodes. I found two separate divisions by zero in the function. Guarding only the first one does not fix all affected cases.  ## Steps to Reproduce  ### 1. Graph with multiple isolated nodes  ```python import networkx as nx  G = nx.Graph() G.add_nodes_from([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])  nx.community.partition_quality(G, [{0, 1}, {2, 3, 4}]) ```  This raises: ZeroDivisionError: division by zero  The failure occurs while calculating coverage:  ```python coverage = intra_community_edges / len(G.edges) ```  The graph has five nodes but no edges, so `len(G.edges) == 0`.  ### 2. Single-node graph  ```python G = nx.Graph() G.add_node(0)  nx.community.partition_quality(G, [{0}]) ```  This also raises a `ZeroDivisionError`. The function later calculates the number of possible node pairs:  ```python total_pairs = n * (n - 1) ```  For one node, `n = 1`, so `total_pairs = 1 * 0 = 0`, and the `performance` calculation divides by zero.  ### 3. Empty graph  ```python G = nx.Graph()  nx.community.partition_quality(G, []) ```  This also raises a `ZeroDivisionError` because `total_pairs` is zero.  ### 4. Directed graph with isolated nodes  ```python D = nx.DiGraph() D.add_nodes_from([0, 1, 2, 3])  nx.community.partition_quality(D, [{0, 1}, {2, 3}]) ```  This raises a `ZeroDivisionError` from the coverage calculation because the graph has no edges.  ## Root Cause  There are two separate zero-division cases in `partition_quality`.  **Coverage:**  ```python coverage = intra_community_edges / len(G.edges) ```  This fails when the graph has no edges.  **Performance:**  ```python total_pairs = n * (n - 1) ```  This becomes zero when the graph has fewer than two nodes, causing the later `performance` calculation to divide by zero.  These conditions are independent. A graph can have many nodes but no edges, so the coverage denominator is zero while the number of possible node pairs is non-zero.

title: Feature Request: Address the zero-similarity problem in `simrank_similarity`
body: ## Summary  `networkx.algorithms.similarity.simrank_similarity` implements Jeh and Widom's original SimRank recursion. This formulation has a known structural defect, the **"zero-similarity" problem**, which causes many structurally related node pairs to receive a similarity score of exactly zero. Therefore, I propose to implement a new similarity function based on **SimRank\*** (Yu et al., VLDBJ 2019), which resolves this problem, and suggests that its closed-form counterpart **PJsim** (Nijhara et al., SIGMOD 2026) be considered as the computational backend, since it removes the iteration/tolerance trade-off that all current SimRank variants in NetworkX are subject to.  ## Background: the zero-similarity problem  Jeh and Widom's SimRank defines similarity recursively:  ``` s(a, b) = 1                                                  if a = b s(a, b) = C / (|I(a)||I(b)|) * sum_{i in I(a), j in I(b)} s(i, j)   if a != b ```  where `I(x)` is the in-neighbor set of `x`. This recursion only accumulates contributions from **symmetric in-link paths**, i.e. paths where the "source" node sits at equal distance from both `a` and `b`. Any path where the source is off-center, and any path of odd length (which can never have a center at all), is entirely ignored, not down-weighted, but ignored. Yu et al. formalize this: SimRank's score `s(a, b)` is zero **if and only if** there is no symmetric in-link path between `a` and `b` in the graph, regardless of how strongly connected `a` and `b` actually are.  On real citation and social graphs this is not an edge case. Yu et al. report that on a citation network (`cit-HepPh`), roughly 97.9% of node pairs are affected by "zero-similarity," and similar magnitudes show up on DBLP-derived graphs. This means `simrank_similarity` today silently returns 0.0 for the overwhelming majority of pairs on typical directed graphs, because the recursion structurally cannot see the paths connecting them.  ## Proposed fix: SimRank\*  Yu et al. propose

body: @rossbar @dschult Thanks for the clarification. While independently verifying my MCB implementation, I found a gap in the current test coverage.  **The gap:** the existing `minimum_cycle_basis` tests use hardcoded snapshot comparisons. Since MCBs are not necessarily unique, these tests are useful as regression snapshots, but they cannot by themselves verify whether an independently produced basis is mathematically valid. title: BUG: bfs_successors yields (node, []) for nodes with no successors
body: `bfs_successors` always performs a final `yield (parent, children)`  after iterating over `bfs_edges`, even when no successors were discovered.  As a result, when the source node has no successors, (example: an isolated node or a sink node in a `DiGraph`), the function returns `(source, [])`.  This contradicts the documented contract, which states: > "`successors` is the non-empty list of successors of `node`. > To appear in the iterator, `node` must have successors."  ## Steps to Reproduce  ```python import networkx as nx  # isolated node G = nx.Graph() G.add_node(0) list(nx.bfs_successors(G, source=0))  # returns [(0, [])] — expected []  # sink node in DiGraph D = nx.DiGraph([(0, 1)]) list(nx.bfs_successors(D, source=1))  # returns [(1, [])] — expected [] ```

title: Audit: 218 functions in 98 files have @not_implemented_for placed outside @_dispatchable (decorator order)
body: ## Summary  An automated audit of the codebase found **218 functions across 98 files** where `@not_implemented_for` is placed **outside** (above) `@nx._dispatchable`. The correct order should be `@_dispatchable` outermost, `@not_implemented_for` inner — because the dispatch system should get first crack at the graph before type restrictions are checked.  ```python # WRONG (218 functions): @not_implemented_for("directed") @nx._dispatchable def my_func(G): ...  # CORRECT (1 function): @nx._dispatchable @not_implemented_for("directed") def my_func(G): ... ```  ## Why it matters  `@_dispatchable` must be outermost because its job is to intercept calls with backend graph objects and redirect them. When `@not_implemented_for` sits outside, the type check runs first on the raw (possibly backend) graph object — if the backend graph doesn't inherit from NetworkX graph classes, it gets rejected before dispatch ever has a chance to convert it.  Today this is likely harmless because most backends (nx-cugraph, etc.) make their graph types inherit from NetworkX classes, so the `isinstance` checks pass. But it's technically incorrect and would silently break any backend using non-inheriting wrappers.  ## Data  | Metric | Count | |---|---| | Files with both decorators | 107 | | Wrong order (`@nif` outside `@dispatch`) | **98 (91.6%)** | | Correct order (`@dispatch` outside `@nif`) | 1 | | Total wrong functions | **218** |  The only file with correct order: `networkx/algorithms/perfect_graph.py` L12 (`is_perfect_graph`).  ## Per-file breakdown  - **networkx/algorithms/approximation/clique.py** (4): `maximum_independent_set`, `max_clique`, `clique_removal`, `large_clique_size` - **networkx/algorithms/approximation/clustering_coefficient.py** (1): `average_clustering` - **networkx/algorithms/approximation/density.py** (1): `densest_subgraph` - **networkx/algorithms/approximation/dominating_set.py** (1): `min_weighted_dominating_set` - **networkx/algorithms/approximation/kcomponents.py

title: Performance: _triangles_and_degree_iter rebuilds neighbor sets redundantly, slowing clustering()
body: Summary nx.clustering() on undirected, unweighted graphs spends most of its time in the internal helper _triangles_and_degree_iter in networkx/algorithms/cluster.py. Profiling shows that a significant amount of that time is redundant work: the same node's neighbor set is reconstructed many times.  How it was found I profiled nx.clustering() on a 2000-node random graph using cProfile. Almost all runtime was inside _triangles_and_degree_iter. The hot line was the generator expression that builds set(G[w]) for each neighbor w. It had the highest self-time and was called over 41,000 times.  Root cause In the inner loop, set(G[w]) is rebuilt every time w is encountered. Since a node appears as a neighbor of each of its own neighbors, its neighbor set gets reconstructed roughly degree-many times over the full computation, even though it never changes.  Proposed fix Precompute each node's neighbor set once into a dictionary before the loop, then reuse it inside the loop instead of rebuilding set(G[w]) each time. The algorithm and output stay exactly the same; only the redundant set construction is removed.  Measured impact Single-core speedup with identical output, verified across multiple graph families (best of several runs): Random sparse 1k nodes 2.56x, Random sparse 3k 3.62x, Random dense 1.5k 3.82x, Scale-free 3k 3.73x, Small-world 3k 2.16x, Complete 200 2.37x. Denser graphs benefit more because neighbor sets are reused more often.  Notes No public API change and output is identical. The existing test_cluster.py suite passes (56 passed). I am happy to open a PR with the change, which is already prepared.

body: ### Hi all  First, thanks for maintaining NetworkX — without this library, I couldn't graduate my degree \😆  I recently noticed something from my advisor and a colleague, and I think it might be a leftover from very early NetworkX. Wanted to flag it gently in case it's worth tidying up.  ### The observation  ```python import networkx as nx  D = nx.DiGraph() D.add_edges_from([(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3), (3, 1)])  nx.degree_centrality(D) # {1: 1.5, 2: 1.0, 3: 1.5}   ← values exceed 1.0 ```  The docstring describes degree centrality as *"the fraction of nodes a node is connected to"*, which naturally implies a `[0, 1]` range. But for `DiGraph`, the current implementation sums `in_degree + out_degree` (max `2(N-1)`) and divides by `N-1`, so the output lives in `[0, 2]`. A small legacy artifact rather than an intentional design choice, I think.  ### Why I think it's worth a small fix  1. The Notes section already calls out multigraphs and self-loops as range exceptions, but not the directed case — so users are likely to assume `[0, 1]` holds. 3. NetworkX already provides `in_degree_centrality` and `out_degree_centrality`, so the natural fix is just to point users there.  ### Suggested fix (minimal, non-breaking)  Just add a friendly warning + a docstring note. body: ## Proposal  I would like to propose adding a backend-only `nx.community.infomap_communities()` API to NetworkX, following the same general model as `leiden_communities()`.  The goal is **not** to add Infomap as a NetworkX dependency and not to port the existing Infomap implementation into NetworkX core. The goal is to let NetworkX define a small, stable community-detection API that installable backends can implement.  A user-facing call would look like:  ```python import networkx as nx  communities = nx.community.infomap_communities(     G,     weight="weight",     seed=123,     backend="infomap", ) ```  and return a `list[set]` partition of `G.nodes`, matching the convention used by `louvain_communities()` and `leiden_communities()`.  ## Why this belongs in NetworkX  NetworkX already provides `louvain_communities()` and a backend-only `leiden_communities()` API. body: ## Summary  A narrowly-scoped follow-up to #4792 (which the maintainers explicitly closed in favor of documentation, [networkx/networkx#6212](https://github.com/networkx/networkx/pull/6212)). I'm **not** proposing to revisit the `tol`/`N*tol` semantic decision. I'm proposing a `RuntimeWarning` for the regime where the threshold is mathematically incapable of gating anything.  ## The math  `pagerank` and `_pagerank_scipy` declare convergence when  ``` err = sum(abs(x[n] - xlast[n]) for n in x)  # L1 distance err < N * tol ```  Both `x` and `xlast` are probability vectors (sum to 1, all entries ≥ 0). The L1 distance between two such vectors is bounded by 2, achieved when their supports are disjoint. So the convergence check is provably equivalent to `True` whenever `N * tol >= 2`. title: nx.display drawing performance for edges
body: This is one topic uncovered an attempt to convert the example gallery from `nx.draw` -> `nx.display`.  `display` performs significantly worse than `draw` w.r.t. edge drawing to the point where it is prohibitive for visualizing modest (>=1000 edges) graphs. An example (should be copy/pasteable to ipython):  ```python >>> G = nx.barabasi_albert_graph(400, m=3, seed=19320) >>> pos = nx.spring_layout(G, iterations=100, seed=5040) >>> nx.set_node_attributes(G, pos, name="pos") >>> %timeit -n1 -r1 nx.draw(G, pos=pos, with_labels=True); >>> %timeit -n1 -r1 nx.display(G); ```  This gives 248 ms vs. 15 sec, respectively on my machine.  This is almost certainly due to logic in `display` choosing FancyArrowPatches for edge drawing as opposed to LineCollection, which is much faster. `draw` chooses LineCollection by default for undirected graphs and `FancyArrowPatch` for directed graphs, with the option to override the default behavior with `arrows`. This logic should be extended to `display` to ensure comparable performance.

title: Benchmark PR workflow fails with build isolation + `--no-index`
body: The benchmark PR workflow can fail while building ASV environments when pip build isolation is enabled together with `--no-index`.  Example failing run: https://github.com/networkx/networkx/actions/runs/24966887015/job/73103123748?pr=8637  The failure is:  ```text pip._vendor.pyproject_hooks._impl.BackendUnavailable: Cannot import 'setuptools.build_meta' ```  The benchmark config currently runs:  ```bash PIP_NO_BUILD_ISOLATION=false python -mpip wheel --no-deps --no-index -w {build_cache_dir} {build_dir} ```  With build isolation enabled, pip creates a temporary build environment and tries to install the build requirements from `pyproject.toml`, including `setuptools>=77.0.3`. Since `--no-index` is set and no local wheelhouse is provided, pip cannot install the build backend into that isolated environment.  Two possible fixes:  1. Disable build isolation for the ASV wheel build, relying on the build requirements installed in the ASV environment:  ```bash PIP_NO_BUILD_ISOLATION=true python -mpip wheel --no-deps --no-index -w {build_cache_dir} {build_dir} ```  2. Keep build isolation, but provide a local wheelhouse for build requirements:  ```bash python -m pip wheel -w {build_cache_dir}/build-deps 'setuptools>=77.0.3' PIP_NO_BUILD_ISOLATION=false python -mpip wheel --no-deps --no-index --find-links {build_cache_dir}/build-deps -w {build_cache_dir} {build_dir} ```

title: node_link_graph/node_link_data: document that edges are stored under 'links' key, not 'edges'
body: ### Description  `networkx.readwrite.json_graph.node_link_data()` serializes edges under the key `"links"` (not `"edges"`). When reading the JSON back, you must pass `edges="links"` to `node_link_graph()` or access `data["links"]` directly.  This is technically documented in the function signature, but it's a common stumbling block because:  1. The natural assumption is that a graph's edges would be under an `"edges"` key 2. Accessing `data["edges"]` doesn't raise a KeyError (it just doesn't exist), so `data.get("edges", [])` silently returns an empty list 3. The graph loads with all nodes but zero edges, which looks like data corruption rather than a key mismatch  ### Suggestion  A brief note in the `node_link_data` docstring or the JSON graph format docs highlighting that the default key is `"links"` (matching the D3.js convention) and that accessing `"edges"` will silently return nothing would save users debugging time.  ### Example of the gotcha  ```python import networkx as nx from networkx.readwrite import json_graph  G = nx.karate_club_graph() data = json_graph.node_link_data(G)  # This silently returns [] -- no KeyError, no warning edges = data.get("edges", [])  # [] -- oops  # This is correct edges = data["links"]  # [{"source": 0, "target": 1, ...}, ...] ```

title: `topological_sort` behavior with non-DAGs
body: I think this is a documentation issue, but I wanted to raise to hear folks' opinions!  The documentation for `topological_sort` (and `topological_generations`) correctly states that an `NetworkXUnfeasible` exception is raised when the input graph is not a DAG.  *However*, since these are generators, it is important to note that this exception is not raised eagerly. In other words, users may get results from `topological_sort` for graphs that are emphatically not acyclic. For example:  ```python >>> G = nx.DiGraph() >>> nx.add_path(G, range(5)) >>> nx.add_cycle(G, range(10, 15))  # contains a cycle # This isn't necessary, but connect the path to the cycle to # illustrate that this isn't only an issue for fully-disconnected # graphs >>> G.add_edge(1, 10) >>> next(nx.topological_sort(G))  # Note: doesn't raise, despite the cycle 0 ```  IMV this is the generator working as intended - the topological ordering is generated on the fly. It just so happens that the cycle is not detected initially, as `topological_generations` starts from nodes with 0 indegree (i.e. the "start" of the path in this case).  At the least I think this behavior should be documented - the docstring currently makes no mention of *when* the exception might be raised during lazy evaluation; so a user may be tempted to rely on e.g. `next(topological_sort)` to determine whether a cycle exists[^1].  [^1]: This is how I landed on this issue - [this line](https://github.com/networkx/networkx/blob/46a639aeb9bd4db8da444bd6a532df567b9a73cc/networkx/algorithms/dag.py#L114) jumped out to me during review of a different PR.

title: ISMAGS: Directed Graphs Incorrectly Treated as Undirected
body: ### Current Behavior  ISMAGS does not distinguish edge direction when processing directed graphs (DiGraph). When comparing two directed graphs with opposite edge directions, the algorithm incorrectly treats them as isomorphic.  For example, a graph with edge `1 -> 2` is considered isomorphic to a graph with edge `2 -> 1`.  ### Expected Behavior  The ISMAGS algorithm should respect edge direction for directed graphs. Two directed graphs with opposite edge directions should NOT be considered isomorphic.  ### Steps to Reproduce  ```python import networkx as nx from networkx.algorithms import isomorphism  # Graph 1: 1 -> 2 G1 = nx.DiGraph() G1.add_edge(1, 2)  # Graph 2: 2 -> 1 (reverse direction) G2 = nx.DiGraph() G2.add_edge(2, 1)  GM = isomorphism.ISMAGS(G1, G2) result = GM.is_isomorphic()  print(f"ISMAGS result: {result}")  # Currently returns True print(f"Expected: False") Output:  text ISMAGS result: True Expected: False Environment Python version: 3.x NetworkX version: All versions since ISMAGS was introduced  Additional context This bug is documented in the source code with # FIXME directed graphs comments:  File: networkx/algorithms/isomorphism/ismags.py  Line 713: # FIXME directed graphs (edge color calculation treats (u,v) same as (v,u))  Line 809: # FIXME directed graphs (compatible edge search ignores direction)  Line 859: # FIXME directed graphs (neighbor options treat edges as undirected)  Root Cause: The algorithm treats edges in directed graphs the same way it treats edges in undirected graphs, failing to distinguish between incoming and outgoing neighbors.  Note: The standard is_isomorphic function for directed graphs works correctly. This issue is specific to the ISMAGS algorithm.  Impact:  Cybersecurity applications relying on directed graph comparison may produce false results  Social network analysis (influence patterns) could be misidentified  Research results based on directed graph isomorphism may be unreliabl

title: [ENH] Add butterfly counting to bipartite module
body: # [ENH] Add butterfly counting to bipartite module  ## Summary  Butterfly counting is a fundamental bipartite graph analysis primitive with no current implementation in NetworkX's `bipartite` module. I'd like to add two functions:  - `nx.algorithms.bipartite.butterfly_count(G)` — total count of K_{2,2} subgraphs - `nx.algorithms.bipartite.butterfly_count_per_vertex(G)` — per-vertex participation  ---  ## What is a butterfly?  A **butterfly** is a complete bipartite subgraph K_{2,2}: four vertices (two from each partition), all four connected to each other, forming a "rectangle" or "4-cycle with diagonals". It is the bipartite analogue of a triangle in unipartite graphs.  ``` Left   Right   0 ── 2   │╲ ╱│   │ ╳ │   │╱ ╲│   1 ── 3 ```  Nodes `{0, 1, 2, 3}` above form one butterfly.  ---  ## Algorithm  The implementation uses the **wedge-based counting approach** from Sanei-Mehri et al. (KDD 2018) [1]:  1. **Rank** vertices by ascending degree (low-degree vertices first — reduces    redundant enumeration, matches PARBUTTERFLY paper [2]). 2. For each pivot vertex `v`, enumerate all pairs of neighbours `(u1, u2)` —    each pair is a *wedge* centred at `v`. 3. Count how many times each `(u1, u2)` pair appears across all pivots.    If pair `(u1, u2)` appears `k` times → `C(k, 2) = k*(k-1)//2` butterflies.  **Complexity:** O(Σ_v d(v)²) time, O(E) space.  ---  ## Proposed API  ```python import networkx as nx  G = nx.Graph() G.add_nodes_from([0, 1], bipartite=0) G.add_nodes_from([2, 3], bipartite=1) G.add_edges_from([(0, 2), (0, 3), (1, 2), (1, 3)])  # Total count nx.bipartite.butterfly_count(G) # → 1  # Per-vertex participation nx.bipartite.butterfly_count_per_vertex(G) # → {0: 1, 1: 1, 2: 1, 3: 1} ```  The functions follow existing conventions in `nx.bipartite`: - Accept an optional `nodes` parameter to specify the pivot partition explicitly - Work on disconnected bipartite graphs (uses BFS 2-coloring as fallback,   not `bipartite.sets()` which raises `AmbiguousSolution` on

title: Some thoughts after using Panther/Panther++
body: I finally had a chance to take both for a spin, and I found a few small surprises/inconsistencies: - Looking at the paper again, the sample size formula uses `C(T, 2)` where `T` is the number of nodes in a path. The way we're generating paths, we're calling `math.comb(path_length, 2)`, but `path_length` is the _edge count_, not the node count, this means we're missing sample paths (`C(5,2) = 10` vs `C(6,2) = 15`).   - The fix would be a simple `t_choose_2 = math.comb(path_length + 1, 2)`. - Because `index_map` is populated only with nodes that appear in at least one sampled path, for a disconnected graph with a sufficiently small `R`, you can get a `KeyError` if you try to access a node that was never visited (`index_map[vi]`).   - I think the likelihood of hitting this is pretty low since we remove isolates in `panther_similarity` and we have a guard against isolates on `panther_vector_similarity`, but it's an easy fix of just `index_map.get(source, set())`   - I'm also wondering whether we should handle isolates in `panther_vector_similarity` (as we do in `panther_similarity`) instead of refusing. A graph like `{0-1, 0-2, 3(isolated)}` with `source=0` is perfectly valid for similarity computation. - Per the paper, we probably want `math.ceil` instead of `int` -- this "off-by-one" has a negligible impact in practice, but I missed that the formula for `R` is giving a lower bound. - In #4400, I said  > Note: I didn't reuse the epsilon parameter because for a sufficiently small graph, that value could be 1.0, which I think would be entirely too large for a reasonable epsilon. title: floyd_warshall breaks backward compatibility: self-loop edges overwrite dist[u][u] = 0
body: This issue was detected by our testing tool and confirmed after discussion between two developers. ### Current Behavior When calling `nx.floyd_warshall` on a graph that contains self-loop edges, the self-distance `dist[u][u]` is incorrectly set to the weight of the self-loop edge (e.g., 5) instead of being fixed to 0. This causes assertion failures and breaks shortest path correctness.  ### Expected Behavior The self-distance `dist[u][u]` **must always be 0** for every node `u`, regardless of whether a self-loop edge exists or what its weight is. Self-loop edges should not overwrite the self-distance. This is a fundamental invariant of the Floyd-Warshall algorithm.  ### Steps to Reproduce ```python import networkx as nx  # Create a directed graph with a self-loop on node 2 G = nx.DiGraph() G.add_weighted_edges_from([(0, 1, 2), (1, 2, 3), (3, 4, 1), (4, 5, 2)]) G.add_edge(2, 2, weight=5)  # Self-loop with weight 5  # Run Floyd-Warshall dist = nx.floyd_warshall(G)  # This assertion FAILS after the regression assert dist[2][2] == 0, f"Expected 0 self-distance, got {dist[2][2]}"  Environment Python version: 3.8+NetworkX version: main branch (after PR #8386) / master branch Additional context This is a breaking regression introduced in PR #8386 ("Floyd Warshall: Adding support for weight parameter as a callable"). Before PR #8386: dist[u][u] = 0 was always preserved, even with self-loops. After PR #8386: The new initialization logic in _init_pred_dist does not skip self-loop edges and overwrites dist[u][u] = 0. This issue is still present in the latest master/main branch and has not been fixed. All existing code using floyd_warshall with self-loops is now broken.

title: Review the threshold graph tools in NetworkX
body: The threshold graph tools in networkx (`algorithms/threshold.py`) have been neglected over the years. Some functions (like `spectral_projection` see #8572) are not tested. And its not clear that many of the functions should be retained.   The goal of the set of functions is/was to provide a way to approximate large complex networks with threshold graph networks allowing a way to get approximate properties and dynamics using the cheap algorithms for e.g. eigenvectors. I doubt that threshold graphs are useful as exact representations (diameter is <= 2). And while computing many network properties is fast that doesn't mean they are good approximations of more complicated networks.  We should remove or update the code in this module.

title: Magnetic Laplacian for Spectral Info
body: Magnetic Graphs are graphs with complex weights, they have a lot of explanations from a physics and some explaniations in terms of matrices from the ML comunity. I want to add a formal introduction from the Magnetic Graphs in a general and structured way in case this propose seems interesting.   This PR suggests adding `magnetic_laplacian_matrix` and `magnetic_laplacian_spectrum` to `networkx/linalg/`, extending NetworkX's spectral tools to directed graphs via the magnetic Laplacian.  **Background** The magnetic Laplacian $L^{(q)}$ is a complex Hermitian matrix associated to a directed graph $G=(V,E)$. Given a parameter $q\in [0, 1/2]$, it is defined as:  $$ L^{(q)} = D - A^{(q)}$$  where D is the degree of  the underlying undirected graph, and $A^{(q)}$ is the Hermitian Magnetic Adjacency Matrix defined as   $$A^{(q)}_{jk} = e^{2\pi iq\theta_{jk}}\cdot \mathbf{1}_{(j,k)\in \tilde{E}}$$  where $\tilde{E}$ is the set of edges adding the other directions and $\theta_{jk}$ is either 1, -1 or 0 if the edge $(i,j)$ is in the specified direction, oposite or in both in $E$ respectively. Then, $L^{(q)}$ has a spectral descomposition.  This construction appears in Shubin (1994) in a differential-geometric context and was later applied to graph analysis by Fanuel et al. (2017) and to graph neural networks by Zhang et al. (2021, MagNet). The parameter q controls how much directional information is encoded: larger q amplifies asymmetry in the spectrum.  **Motivation** NetworkX doesn't provide any tool to work with this kind of graphs, and they are very useful. I will also like to scale this PR to classes of functions over the nodes (signals) and over the edges and relate them with differentiation operators. If this issue seems interesting I will add a formal and structured introduction of Magnetic Graph and basic functions.

title: `maximal_independent_set` returns a list
body: This is not a bug in a strict sense - the nodes in the list do comprise a maximal independent set - but it is strange (and arguably semantically inconsistent) to return a list of nodes instead of a set.  Though it'd technically be a breaking change, I think my vote would be to update the implementation to return a set instead of a list. If we wanted to be cautious, we could raise a FutureWarning; the downside is I can't think of a way to give a "do X to make this warning go away & future-proof your code" recipe, at least not without introducing new API (which I'm -1 on).  I'd be inclined to simply change it without a runtime warning.  **Context**  I ran into this while attempting to show that a mis returned by `maximal_independent_set` is (often) just one of many possible maximal independent sets; i.e.  ```python >>> G = nx.path_graph(4) >>> G.add_edges_from([(1, 4), (2, 4)])  # Add a triangle >>> mis = nx.maximal_independent_set(G) >>> all_mis = { ...     frozenset(c) ...     for c in nx.enumerate_all_cliques(nx.complement(G)) ...     if len(c) > 1 ... } >>> mis in all_mis  # this is where I ran into the issue Traceback (most recent call last)    ... body: A while back we wrote a wrapper for RandomState objects to be allowed with functions that use the python.random API.  We didn't cover all possible methods of Python's `random` object because that would be a moving target. So we restricted it to methods we actually used. This is documented in the code for `py_random_state` and friends.  The idea is that new contributions should be able to use new Python `random` methods. Then when a user tries to input `seed=np.random.RandomState(42)` they get an AttributeError. Note that this must be new code they are writing (newer than the NX code which calls the random method), so they should be using `np.random.Generators` instead of `RandomState`.    This issue tries to make that easier on a user by catching and re-raising the AttributeError with a message reminding the user to use a Generator rather than a RandomState object.  See also #8514   Alternative: - we could update the wrapper when new code uses a Python `random` method not wrapped by the wrapper.

title: enh: ~2x speedup for unweighted betweenness_centrality with implementation-level optimizations
body:
I’ve been experimenting with implementation-level optimizations for the unweighted ‎`betweenness_centrality` routine and found a set of pure-Python changes that give about a 1.9x geometric mean speedup over the current NetworkX implementation, with identical outputs on all the graphs I tested. This does not change the algorithm (still Brandes, still ‎`O(VE)`), only how it is implemented. All benchmarks are against NetworkX 3.4.2 on Python 3.12.9 (Darwin/ARM). I tested ER, BA, and WS graphs between 100 and 5000 nodes. Example results (time in seconds): Graph | Nodes | Edges | NetworkX | Optimized | Speedup -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- random (ER) | 100 | 269 | 0.013 | 0.007 | 1.90x scale-free (BA) | 500 | 1,494 | 0.236 | 0.140 | 1.68x random (ER) | 1,000 | 3,011 | 1.205 | 0.605 | 1.99x scale-free (BA) | 2,000 | 5,994 | 4.537 | 2.498 | 1.82x random (ER) | 5,000 | 15,054 | 40.107 | 18.205 | 2.20x scale-free (BA) | 5,000 | 14,994 | 35.237 | 17.656 | 2.00x Across all 14 configurations, the geometric mean speedup is about 1.9x. For each graph configuration, I compare against ‎`networkx.betweenness_centrality`: - Max absolute difference between centrality values: 0.0 (bit-for-bit identical in my tests) - Kendall tau rank correlation ≥ 0.9988; the small deviations occur only on random graphs where many nodes have nearly identical scores, so ordering is sensitive to floating-point tie-breaking.

What changed (code-level)

These changes are all in the inner BFS + dependency accumulation for the unweighted case.

  1. Dict → list/array indexing

Before (dicts keyed by nodes):

P = {v: [] for v in adj}        # dict of lists   sigma = {v: 0.0 for v in adj}   # dict of floats   D = {}                          # dict of ints

After (integer-indexed lists):

P = [[] for _ in range(n)]      # list of lists (indexed by int)   sigma = [0.0] * n

title: Computing normalized rich-club coefficient may lead to `ZeroDivisionError`
body: ### Current Behavior In certain instances, computation of the normalised rich club coefficient may lead to a `ZeroDivisionError`. This is more likely to happen for sparse graphs with a relatively low number of high-degree nodes.   The `ZeroDivisionError` occurs as part of the normalisation in `rich_club_coefficient` when the rich club coefficent is 0 for the randomised graph but not for the original graph:  https://github.com/networkx/networkx/blob/44211b8b182ff44a541a191f9b72007082f5bd26/networkx/algorithms/richclub.py#L99  ### Expected Behavior The referenced works by McAuley et al. and Milo et al. are not explicit about this phenomenon. Two main suggestions for resolving the bug can be found below.   **Option 1**: Returning `NaN` values for unclear values:  ```diff - rc = {k: v / rcran[k] for k, v in rc.items()} + rc = {k: v / rcran[k] if rcran[k] != 0 else math.nan for k, v in rc.items()} ```  **Option 2**: Reducing the length of the returned array in case the randomised graph has zero values: ```diff + rc = rc[:next((i for i, x in enumerate(rcran) if x == 0), len(rcran))] ```  ### Steps to Reproduce  A minimum example can be found below:  ```py graph = networkx.Graph(directed=False) graph.add_node("A") graph.add_node("A_1") graph.add_node("A_2") graph.add_node("B") graph.add_node("B_1") graph.add_node("B_2") graph.add_node("C") graph.add_node("D") graph.add_edge("A", "A_1") graph.add_edge("A", "A_2") graph.add_edge("B", "B_1") graph.add_edge("B", "B_2") graph.add_edge("A", "B") graph.add_edge("C", "D")  for i in range(1000):     networkx.rich_club_coefficient(graph, normalized=True, Q=1) ```  ### Environment Python version: 3.13.7 NetworkX version: 3.2.1

title: Optimize _build_paths_from_predecessors stack logic for 30-40% speedup
body: ### Description This PR optimizes the `_build_paths_from_predecessors` function in `networkx/algorithms/shortest_paths/generic.py`. The current implementation manages the stack manually using list indices (`stack[top][1] = i + 1`), which is verbose and adds overhead. I have refactored this to use a standard iterator-based stack approach (`stack = [[node, iter(children)]]`). Memory: Uses python iterators which are generally more memory-efficient than maintaining explicit index integers for every stack level, though the difference is likely negligible compared to the graph size. ### Improvements 1. **Performance:** Consistently **30-40% faster** on large graphs. 2. **Readability:** Reduces code complexity by removing manual index tracking and explicit "top" pointer manipulation. ### Benchmark Results I benchmarked both implementations using `nx.grid_2d_graph(N, N)` from $N=2$ to $N=16$. The new implementation shows significant time savings as the number of paths grows. **Test Environment:** Grid Graph (NxN), finding all shortest paths from `(0,0)` to `(N-1, N-1)`. | Grid Size | Paths Found | Old Time (s) | New Time (s) | Speedup | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **10x10** | 48,620 | 0.190s | 0.105s | **1.80x** | | **12x12** | 705,432 | 2.55s | 1.52s | **1.68x** | | **14x14** | 10,400,600 | 38.93s | 22.21s | **1.75x** | | **15x15** | 40,116,600 | 153.65s | 85.30s | **1.80x** | | **16x16** | 155,117,520 | 795.19s | 494.92s | **1.61x** | **Total Time Saved (16x16):** ~300 seconds (5 minutes). ### Performance Graph ### Implementation Details **Old Approach:** ```python seen = {target} stack = [[target, 0]] top = 0 while top >= 0: node, i = stack[top] if node in sources: yield [p for p, n in reversed(stack[: top + 1])] if len(pred[node]) > i: stack[top][1] = i + 1 next = pred[node][i]

title: [Feature Request] Add count_motifs function using ESU algorithm for subgraph enumeration
body: ### Feature Description  I would like to propose adding a [count_motifs] function to NetworkX for counting connected induced subgraph motifs using the ESU (Enumerate Subgraphs) algorithm.  ### Motivation / Use Cases  NetworkX currently only has `triadic_census` for counting k=3 triads in **directed** graphs. There is no general-purpose function for: - Counting motifs of arbitrary sizes (k=2, 3, 4) - Working with **undirected** graphs - Returning counts grouped by isomorphism class  **Use cases include:** - Biological network analysis (protein interaction networks, gene regulatory networks) - Social network motif detection - Network comparison using motif frequency profiles - Structural pattern mining in graphs  ### Proposed API  ```python from networkx import count_motifs  G = nx.complete_graph(4) motifs = count_motifs(G, size=3) # Returns: {'<canonical_hash>': 4}  # 4 triangles in K4  G = nx.path_graph(4)   motifs = count_motifs(G, size=3) # Returns: {'<hash>': 2}  # 2 connected 3-node induced subgraphs ``` #### Parameters:  - `G` : NetworkX Graph or DiGraph - size : int (default=3, range 2-4) — number of nodes in the motif  #### Returns: - `dict[str, int]` — mapping of canonical subgraph hash to occurrence count  #### Algorithm The ESU algorithm (Wernicke, 2006) is a well-established method for exact subgraph enumeration:  - Efficient: avoids duplicate counting via ordered node traversal - Memory-efficient: uses depth-first search without storing all subgraphs - Canonical labeling: uses Weisfeiler-Lehman graph hash (already in NetworkX)  #### Reference:  "Wernicke, S. (2006). Efficient Detection of Network Motifs. IEEE/ACM Transactions on Computational Biology and Bioinformatics, 3(4), 347-359."  #### Implementation Status I have already worked on: - Supports directed and undirected graphs - Handles non-integer node labels - Includes 13 test cases - Passes all ruff checks - Includes docstrings and doctests

title: 'circular_ladder_graph'  returns incorrect graph for n < 2 (creates spurious nodes and self-loops)
body: #### Current Behavior  circular_ladder_graph(n) produces incorrect results for small values of n: 1. circular_ladder_graph(0) creates nodes [0, -1] with an edge between them, instead of returning an empty graph 2. circular_ladder_graph(1) creates self-loops (0, 0) and (1, 1) in addition to the valid edge (0, 1).  This occurs because the function unconditionally adds edges (0, n-1) and  (n, 2*n-1) without checking if n >= 2. When n=0, this evaluates to add_edge(0, -1) which creates two spurious nodes. When n=1, this evaluates to add_edge(0, 0) and add_edge(1, 1) which creates self-loops.  #### Expected Behavior 1.circular_ladder_graph(0) should return an empty graph with 0 nodes and 0 edges (consistent with ladder_graph(0)) 2. circular_ladder_graph(1) should return a graph with 2 nodes and 1 edge (0, 1) , with no self-loops (consistent with ladder_graph(1))  #### Steps to Reproduce ```python import networkx as nx  # Test n=0: creates spurious nodes G = nx.circular_ladder_graph(0) print("n=0 nodes:", list(G.nodes()))  # Output: [0, -1] - should be [] print("n=0 edges:", list(G.edges()))  # Output: [(0, -1)] - should be []  # Test n=1: creates self-loops G = nx.circular_ladder_graph(1) print("n=1 nodes:", list(G.nodes()))  # Output: [0, 1] print("n=1 edges:", list(G.edges()))  # Output: [(0, 1), (0, 0), (1, 1)] - should be [(0, 1)]  # Compare with ladder_graph which handles these cases correctly print("ladder_graph(0) nodes:", list(nx.ladder_graph(0).nodes()))  # Output: [] print("ladder_graph(1) nodes:", list(nx.ladder_graph(1).nodes()))  # Output: [0, 1] print("ladder_graph(1) edges:", list(nx.ladder_graph(1).edges()))  # Output: [(0, 1)] ``` #### Environment Python version: 3.11 NetworkX version: 3.6 / main branch  #### Additional context The fix is straightforward - add a check if n >= 2: before adding the closing edges that connect the two cycles. I have already prepared a fix with tests and can submit a PR.

title: API: deprecate `maximum_flow_value` and `minimum_cut_value`?
body: See #8392   There are two functions in the `maxflow` submodule that have associated `_value` function definitions: `nx.maximum_flow`/`nx.maximum_flow_value` and `nx.minimum_cut`/ `nx.minimum_cut_value`.  In both cases, the `_value` version is identical, but only returns the computed value instead of the value + flow dict (both are computed in both cases).  Obviously the corresponding `_value` function could by deprecated in favor of argument unpacking, e.g.  ```python flow_value = nx.maximum_flow_value(G, src, tgt, capacities) ```  can be replaced with  ```python flow_value, _ = nx.maximum_flow(G, src, tgt, capacities) ```  The main advantage of doing so (from my perspective) is eliminating the possibility that the function and it's `_value` counterpart fall out of sync. #8392 accomplishes this in terms of implementation, but there are still docstrings etc. The downside, as always, is disrupting user code. title: Performance could be increased for _dijkstra_multisource
body: In `_dijkstra_multisource` there are a number of ways to increase speed.  I expect that we could get substantial speedups with a variety of modifications some of which would have other ramifications, but should still be considered.  The two largest culprits slowing the algorithm appear to be:  - Predecessors are stored as a dict of lists such that equal lengths to a single node can both be added as a predecessor.     - This Forces the creation and modification of lists a substantial amount of times during the algorithm runtime.     - List creation and modification is much slower than simply swapping an `int` at a dictionary location.     - A potential speedup without affecting function would be to only create the list once and `clear` it instead of creating a new list object.      - You could achieve a substantial speedup by instead storing only the most recent predecessor.     - Since many algorithms do not need the predecessor, but paths, we can make a nice speedup by only following the original predecessor tracking process if it is needed to avoid breaking changes. Then we can store a single ref predecessor dict for path reconstruction if needed with a substantial speedup on storing and access. - The weight function is called during iterations.     - If we could have an alternative graph form like `_adj` but with the form of:  ``` {     'my_weight_1':{0:{1:5.0},1:{0:5.0}}     'my_weight_2':{0:{1:2.0},1:{0:2.0}} } ```     - We could avoid the function call for single variable weight functions (which are likely the most common).     - Instead we could just pass the graph in and this should cut times substantially   Given these first two suggestions, I expect we could cut run times in half or more (unless the original predecessor tracking is needed).  Further speedup suggestions:  - Offer single predecessor tracking instead of multi predecessor tracking such that people who don't care about multiple predecessors can still get substantial speedups. - Convert to solvi

title: Deprecate metric_closure
body: Following up on [discussion #8294](https://github.com/networkx/networkx/discussions/8294)  The metric_closure function currently lives in networkx/algorithms/approximation/steinertree.py, but:  - It is not used by any of the Steiner tree algorithms (originally added for Kou’s algorithm, but later replaced). - Having it under the approximation namespace is misleading, since metric_closure is a general graph transformation (complete graph with shortest-path distances), not an approximation routine. - The same functionality is essentially available via all_pairs_shortest_path_length, so the dedicated function provides limited additional value.  Proposed changes:  - Add a DeprecationWarning to metric_closure. - Add .. deprecated:: directive in the docstring. - Update release notes to mention planned removal in the next major release. - Add a small gallery example to illustrate the “metric closure” terminology and show that it corresponds to computing all-pairs shortest path lengths.

title: [Feature Request] Add Directed Steiner Tree Approximation (Charikar et al. 1999)
body: Hi, I’m a first-time contributor and I’m currently working on a project related to satellite networks. title: centroid vs barycenter in distance_measures and tree.distance_measures
body: We successfully made a function `nx.tree.tree_centroid` (#8089) which is called from `nx.barycenter` when the input graph is a tree. We have also implemented a function `nx.tree.center` (#8174) which is called from `nx.center` (#8174) when the input graph is a tree.  Let's merge those two PRs and work out the details of the bigger-picture API in this issue and follow-up PRs. It'd be nice to get these ll sorted out before the next release so we don't have to deprecate the newly introduced functions.  **Centroid vs Barycenter** I've looked into this a little, and my impressions include:  1) that the Barycenter of a graph is a subgraph, not a set of nodes. But our function returns a set of nodes.  2) It looks like barycenter, centroid, and median (or maybe weighted median which seems like a self-contradiction to me) all refer to the same concept.  3) The term `centroid` seems to have the most links and connected ideas, other than in networkx.  These impressions are somewhat subjective, so happy to be corrected or nudged to different perspectives. On an even more speculative level, it seems to me that "barycenter" and "median" have a harder time connecting to other literature -- and spend more time explaining what they mean, often without a clear definition (especially "barycenter"). The centroid literature seems more extensive and connected.  - [ ] I propose that we use the name "centroid" in both `tree.distance_measures.py` and `distance_measures.py`. But, we should keep `nx.barycenter` as an alias to centroid, and use all three names in the docs.  - [x] In the tree subpackage we should rename `tree_centroid` as `centroid` before the next release. - [ ] It'd be nice to keep the api features (like `sp` input of shortest_paths dict and output of nodes rather than induced subgraphs) of the current functions.

title: ENH: Add function for Hyper-Wiener Index
body: ### Proposal  New function, `networkx.hyper_wiener_index(G)`, to calculate the Hyper-Wiener Index of a graph.  The Hyper-Wiener Index ($WW$) is a well-known topological index used in chemical graph theory. It's a natural extension of the existing `nx.wiener_index`. Adding this function would enhance the library's utility for structure-property studies.  ### Proposed Implementation  The index is defined by the formula: $$WW(G) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{u, v \in V(G)} [d(u,v) + d(u,v)^2]$$ where $d(u,v)$ is the shortest path distance between vertices $u$ and $v$.  This can be implemented efficiently by iterating through the results of `nx.all_pairs_shortest_path_length(G)`.  For consistency with `nx.wiener_index`, the function should raise a `NetworkXError` if the input graph is not connected.  I have already started working on this feature and will submit a pull request for review shortly.  ### References * [Wikipedia: Hyper-Wiener Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyper-Wiener_index) * Randić, M. (1993). Novel molecular descriptor for structure-property studies. *Chemical Physics Letters, 211*(4-5), 478-483.

title: `edges_equal` implicitly assumes edges are undirected
body: While working on #8077, I realised `edges_equal` currently duplicates edges when building the attribute dictionaries for each edge. https://github.com/networkx/networkx/blob/9f8e7e298828ced14200e6bdabcd6d02f5965cec/networkx/utils/misc.py#L540-L546  This means that directed graphs that only differ in the direction of their edges are handled incorrectly: ```python-console >>> import networkx as nx >>> G = nx.DiGraph([(0, 1)]) >>> H = nx.DiGraph([(1, 0)]) >>> nx.utils.edges_equal(G.edges, H.edges) True ```  This behavior is not necessarily intuitive—nothing about the function name or even description mentions the directedness of edges. This leaves the following options: 1. Always assume edges are directed, but that would be backward incompatible. 2. Add an argument specifying whether edges should be considered as directed or not, although that brings up the issue of what to do if only one of the edge lists given is directed (add a flag for each edge list?) 3. Explicitly clarify that edge directedness is ignored in the docstring, as is done with the order of the edges. This is the simplest solution by far, but it does mean there's a gap in functionality (tools for comparing edges of directed graphs) that I think is reasonable to fill.

title: ENH: `min_length` kwarg for `simple_cycles`

I wonder if it might be possible to add related functionality: i.e. a `minimum_length` keyword to yield cycles that are at least a certain length.  Of course, this could naively be done with a simple filter `[c for c in nx.simple_cycles(G) if len(c) > minimum_length]`, but what I'm interested in is whether there are any *algorithmic* approaches to only finding cycles above a certain length that are of course more efficient than the full cycle-search.  I haven't done any research on this front, but if such approaches exist I think they could be quite valuable!

title: Improve error message for removed `random_tree` function in NetworkX ≥ 3.4
body: ### Summary  In NetworkX versions < 3.4, the function `networkx.random_tree` was available and widely used for generating random trees. From version 3.4 onward, this function has been **removed**, as per PRs [#7415](https://github.com/networkx/networkx/pull/7415) and [#7411](https://github.com/networkx/networkx/pull/7411).  However, trying to access it now results in a generic and confusing error:  ``` AttributeError: module 'networkx' has no attribute 'random_tree' ```  This error message is **not informative**, especially for users upgrading from older code or referencing existing tutorials or notebooks.  ---  ### Suggestion  I propose adding a small `__getattr__` fallback in `networkx/__init__.py` to raise a clearer message when someone tries to access the removed function.  Example:  ```python def __getattr__(name):     if name == "random_tree":         raise AttributeError(             "`networkx.random_tree` was removed in version 3.4. Use `networkx.random_labeled_tree` instead.\n"             "See: https://networkx.org/documentation/networkx-3.5/release/release_3.4.html"         )     raise AttributeError(f"module 'networkx' has no attribute '{name}'") ```  This change would significantly improve developer experience when debugging legacy code or migrating projects from older versions.  Please let me know if you're open to this. I'm happy to open a PR for this right after!

A backend graph instance may have a G.__networkx_cache__ dict to enable caching, and care should be taken to clear the cache when appropriat ```  However, `_not_implemented_for` decorator is called before dispatching, causing an exception if the graph doesn't implement either `is_multigraph` or `is_directed`.  ```     def _not_implemented_for(g):         if (mval is None or mval == g.is_multigraph()) and (             dval is None or dval == g.is_directed()         ):             raise nx.NetworkXNotImplemented(errmsg)          return g ```  We should probably add that to documents in the short-term but wanted to discuss if this should really be necessary. This forces users to implement those methods which might not be possible in case the class passed is not part of the code base (external library). Of course we can always wrap it like nx_parallel does (https://github.com/networkx/nx-parallel/blob/main/nx_parallel/interface.py#L59) but that adds an extra layer of indirection.  What could be done here? - Make `_not_implemented_for` not raise if is_multigraph/is_directed are not defined? - Change the order of decorators to dispatch before validating the type?

title: `generate_random_paths` should be `generate_random_walks`
body: Two notes about random_paths... - These are walks...  not paths...  The nodes can be repeated. The cited article itself switches between the term `path` and `walk` mid-sentence and doesn't distinguish between them.  The article clearly means walks. But often calls them paths. We should probably change the name here and either deprecate/remove the current name, or provide a random path routine.  I believe random walks are the thing most people use though. - The corner cases where no path exist (like the null graph) or when probabilities don't exist (reciprocal divides by zero) could be handled better but lets do that in a different PR.  First step would be to and `generate_random_walks` and deprecate the current name.   In that PR we can hanlde (or not) the corner cases of null graph and dividing by zero in reciprocal.

title: Improve Girman-Newman speed
body: Girman-Newman method (https://networkx.org/documentation/stable/reference/algorithms/generated/networkx.algorithms.community.centrality.girvan_newman.html) is a hierarchal clustering method that is computationally expensive. This has raised multiple questions from users: - https://stackoverflow.com/questions/62951320/why-is-the-girvan-newman-algorithm-in-networkx-so-slow - https://github.com/networkx/networkx/discussions/7967  Based on the code there might be many optimization opportunities. Some of them could be: - Caching the count of edges inside the algo and updating it on every edge removal. Counting edges is currently linear - Making the algorithm work with one graph per connected components internally (as opposed to a single graph with many components). This way counting connected components is only done on the component being affected by the removal. Another advantage of this would be that metric for edges of unaffected components could be cached.

title: Iteration over MST and CDS and maybe other trees
body: In today's community meeting we discussed iterators over minimum spanning trees (MSTs) and connected dominating sets (CDSs).   **Iterating over MSTs:** Matt pointed out that the spanning tree iterator code he wrote yields the trees in order of size, so one could get all the MSTs by iterating through all the trees of minimum size and then stop when the size of a yielded tree changes. - let's make that more obvious in the docs somehow - maybe we can make a helper function that does this iteration. Or maybe an example in the MST docstring?  **Iterating over CDSs:** Ross brought up the idea that now that we (almost) have some CDS functions, that CDSs are not unique.  We might want an iterator over all CDSs. Alejandro suggested that what is often desired is a minimum CDS.  This could be stated as a CDS associated with a tree that is a MST.  It seems like a possible system for minimum CDSs could be to generate MSTs and from them generate the CDS (by forming the set of nodes that are not leaves of the MST).   If someone wants all minimum CDSs, we could iterate over MSTs and return the CDSs each is associated with (two distinct MSTs might give the same CDS, so we'd need to check for that).

title: Directed edges in MultiDiGraph not handled correctly by subgraph monomorphism
body: ### Current Behavior  A directed graph without edges should not have a subgraph monomorphic to a digraph with one edge. However, current implementation says it is monomorphic.  ### Expected Behavior  It should not be considered monomorphic.  ### Steps to Reproduce  import networkx as nx  G = nx.MultiGraph() G.add_node("A", label="A") G.add_node("B", label="B") H = nx.MultiGraph([["A", "B"]]) # one edge matcher = nx.isomorphism.GraphMatcher(G, H) print(matcher.subgraph_is_monomorphic()) ## False, as expected  G = nx.MultiDiGraph() G.add_node("A", label="A") G.add_node("B", label="B") H = nx.MultiDiGraph([["A", "B"]]) # one edge matcher = nx.isomorphism.GraphMatcher(G, H) print(matcher.subgraph_is_monomorphic()) ## True, should be false  ### Environment  Ubuntu 22.04 inside Windows 10 WSL  Python version: Python 3.12.3 NetworkX version: 3.4.2  ### Additional context  My suspicion as to what is going on:   Say the edge is A -> B. I suspect A is mapped first and added into core_1. A has no mapped neighbor yet that needs to check the edge existence, so it's fine. And when B is mapped and added, it has no (outgoing) neighbors, so the edge is also not checked. The program never notices that the "monomorphism" is missing the directed edge.

title: Cytoscape export of a cartesian graph is invalid
body: The Graph or DiGraph resulting from applying the `cartesian_product` operator is not properly exported to a Cytoscape JSON.   I suspect this has to do with how node labels in the Cartesian product are exported to JSON. In the output, they are represented as a list, and likely only a string is accepted by Cytoscape. (See also minimal example below.) For example, for the Cartesian graph, the JSON has  ```json "edges": [     {         "data": {             "source": [ "a",   "a" ], ```  whereas in the base graph one only has   ```json "source": "a" ```  On the other hand, node IDs in the Cartesian JSON look like `"id": "('a', 'a')"`  Perhaps using a string for the Cartesian case would be a robust solution? So just match how node IDs are represented. I don't know how "complex" node labels can be in Cytoscape but I would guess it's still internally a string, no matter how it's parsed.   ### Current Behavior  When importing the JSON into Cytoscape (via _File > Import > Network from File_), the following error message is displayed "source node is not a member of this network" and no data is loaded. The Cytoscape Java console does not say anything more.  ### Expected Behavior  The (di)graph to be loaded with correct structure and labels.   ### Steps to Reproduce  A trivial graph can be used to reproduce this as below. The `test_cross.json` is the problematic one:  ```python import json import networkx as nx  G = nx.DiGraph() G.add_edge('a', 'b') C = nx.cartesian_product(G, G)  cy_data_graph = nx.cytoscape_data(G) cy_data_cartesian = nx.cytoscape_data(C)  # Using nicely formatted output for diffing exports with open('/tmp/test.json', 'w') as export_file:     export_file.write(json.dumps(cy_data_graph, indent=4))  with open('/tmp/test_cross.json', 'w') as export_file:     export_file.write(json.dumps(cy_data_cartesian, indent=4)) ```  Note that writing with `json.dump(nx.cytoscape_data(C), export_file)` is of course identical, the above is for easy diffing of the JSONs  ### E

title: minimum_st_node_cut returns empty dict instead of empty set
body: ### Current Behavior  If you use the method "minimum_st_node_cut" from connectivity with nodes s and t which are directly connected by an edge, the method returns an empty dictionary instead of an empty set.  This is due to the following code part: ```     if G.has_edge(s, t) or G.has_edge(t, s):         return {} ```  ### Expected Behavior  The method minimum_st_node_cut declares to return a set of nodes.  So I would expect to get a set in this case, too, not a dict.  ```     Returns     -------     cutset : set         Set of nodes that, if removed, would destroy all paths between         source and target in G. ```  Probably just a typo: To create an empty set, you would have to use set(), not {} . So the fix should be:  ```     if G.has_edge(s, t) or G.has_edge(t, s):         return set() ```  ### Steps to Reproduce  ``` G = nx.Graph() G.add_nodes_from(["s", "t"]) G.add_edges_from([("s", "t")]) separator = nx.algorithms.connectivity.minimum_st_node_cut(G, "s", "t") print (type(separator)) ```  ### Environment  Python version: 3.13.1 NetworkX version: 3.4.2  ### Additional context  It may be unexpected to some users to get an empty nodeset if s and t are directly connected by an edge, even if it is described e.g. in Diestel "Graph Theory", 6. ed., Springer 2025, on page 11 that a nodesset is a separator for vertices a and b if it separates those two vertices and doesn't include a and b. So maybe a hint in the documentation that you should check for an edge between s and t before calling this method would be helpful. Or the documentation for this method could include the information that two totally unconnected nodes s and t and two directly connected nodes s and t with an edge "st" or "ts" will both result in an empty set as return value.

title: Bugs WL (sub)graph hashing in relation to use degree at initialisation
body: ### Current Behavior  At initialisation in both `weisfeiler_lehman_graph_hash` and `weisfeiler_lehman_subgraph_hashes` for graphs that do not have node or edge attributes, node weights are initialised using the degree of the nodes. This already aggregates information about neighbours at a 1-hop distance (the direct neighbours).  This has three main consequences. - The explanation and examples in the documentation are incorrect. It gives an example that requires 4 neighbourhood aggregations for certain nodes to converge to the same label, but incorrectly finds only 3 (the aggregation during node initialisation is not visible). - The behaviour of graphs with and without attributes (even if those attributes are trivial/irrelevant) is not in line with each other. This is because graphs with node attributes skip this step. - It hides a bug in the implementation for directed nodes: certain graphs are now correctly distinguished because of this initial step, but fail to be distinguished by graphs with attributes.   ### Expected Behavior  Using a node's degree can be an efficient way to aggregate information about the 1-hop neighbourhood. However, this should then be used as the first iteration, instead of during initialisation. It should not be used for directed graphs (at least not in this way) because apparently it treats outgoing and ingoing edges the same.  Directed graphs should consider both in- and outgoing edges at each iteration of the algorithm.  ### Steps to Reproduce  The iteration problem on undirected graphs: ```python # This is the example used in the documentation. G1 = nx.Graph() G1.add_edges_from([(1, 2), (2, 3), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 6), (5, 7), (6, 7)]) G2 = nx.Graph() G2.add_edges_from([(1, 3), (2, 3), (1, 6), (1, 5), (4, 6)]) g1_hashes = nx.weisfeiler_lehman_subgraph_hashes(G1, iterations=3, digest_size=8) g2_hashes = nx.weisfeiler_lehman_subgraph_hashes(G2, iterations=3, digest_size=8) # diverge at iteration 3" print(g2_hashes[5]) print(g1_hashes[1]) #

body: There seems to be some inconsistency with how NetworkX handles data with pandas>=2.  The main issue here, as described below: > why would NetworkX inconsistently make the edge `u` a Python int but make the edge `v` a `np.int64`?  ### Current vs Expected Behavior  For example, if we run this snippet with Networkx v3.4 and (*old*) pandas v1.5.3:  ```python import networkx as nx import pandas as pd  # nodes come saved as a path in a pandas series nodes = pd.Series([333, 555])  # add the nodes and the edge G = nx.MultiDiGraph() G.add_nodes_from(nodes) G.add_edge(nodes[0], nodes[1])  print(G.nodes)  # [333, 555] print(G.edges)  # [(333, 555, 0)] ``` ...the resulting graph nodes are of type int, and the edge is a tuple of ints, as expected. All good.  However, if we run that snippet again, but this time with Networkx v3.4.2 and (*current*) pandas v2.2.3:  ```python import networkx as nx import pandas as pd  # nodes come saved as a path in a pandas series nodes = pd.Series([333, 555])  # add the nodes and the edge G = nx.MultiDiGraph() G.add_nodes_from(nodes) G.add_edge(nodes[0], nodes[1])  print(G.nodes)  # [333, 555] print(G.edges)  # [(333, np.int64(555), 0)] ``` ...the resulting graph nodes are still of type int, and the edge's `u` is an int, but the edge's `v` is type `np.int64`. Recent versions of pandas use these numpy types, but why would NetworkX inconsistently make the edge `u` a Python int but make the edge `v` a `np.int64`?  ### Environment  Platform: ubuntu 24.10 Python version: 3.11 NetworkX version: 3.4 and 3.4.2 (it appears I cannot install NetworkX>3.4 with pandas>=2)  ### Additional context  @LBasara brought this issue to my attention because it's affecting the OSMnx package downstream (crossref https://github.com/gboeing/osmnx/issues/1241). They also provided this screenshot:   ![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6c65af01-dac0-4f32-978c-f7ab934a4993)

title: Unexpected behavior for subgraph monomorphisms with MultiGraph
body: <!-- If you have a general question about NetworkX, please use the discussions tab to create a new discussion -->  <!--- Provide a general summary of the issue in the Title above --> When using `MultiGraph` the determining of subgraph monomorphisms doesn't work as expected when having multiple edges with different "colors" between two nodes.  ### Current Behavior  <!--- Tell us what happens instead of the expected behavior --> A graph with two nodes connected by two edges with different "color" (encoded as `data` of the edge) is considered to be not subgraph monomorphic to a graph with two nodes connected by only one edge with one of the respective colors.  ### Expected Behavior  I would expect above scenario to be a subgraph monomorphism. title: Linting: enforce line lengths
body: I was under the impression that the pre-commit auto-linters enforced a maximum line length both in code and documentation, and would automatically re-format inputs that violated those rules. However, it appears this isn't currently the case.  For example - if one follows the contributor guide to set up the development environment (including pre-commit) then creates a dummy commit with a line with 120+ characters in it, pre-commit won't complain or try to reformat it.  Was the removal of this feature intentional? I know we adopted black in the past for this very reason and IIRC `ruff format` was intended to supplant black, but it seems we've lost the autofix-line-len-violations feature that we once had. If the removal was intentional, I'd vote to bring it back - it's much more convenient than having to ask contributors to manually keep lines at a certain length.

title: Separation of Exception Handling/Input Validation from Algorithm's Core Implementation
body: During the [Dispatching, Backend Selection, and Compatibility APIs](https://pretalx.com/euroscipy-2024/talk/8MXPRW/) discussion at EuroSciPy 2024 (for reference - https://hackmd.io/@seberg/spatch), it was proposed to separate exception handling and input validation from the core implementation of algorithms. This would result in more maintainable backend code and a better experience for backend developers, and also would reduce redundant code across backend packages. We briefly discussed this in a NetworkX dispatch meeting but never followed up.  ```.py def validator(G, ...):     if not G:          raise nx.NetworkXError("Expected non-empty NetworkX graph!")     return ...          @dispatchable(validator) def nx_func(G, ...):     ... ```  ### Challenges:  - Large-scale refactoring of the main networkx repository's codebase. - Not all exceptions could be handled in the `validator`, like `ExceededMaxIterations`, `PowerIterationFailedConvergence`, etc.(raised in the middle of algorithm's core implementation)  ### Proposed Changes:  - Update the `_dispatchable` decorator to handle the `validator` function. - Start by refactoring only the algorithms implemented in the backends. Gradually refactor other algorithms as we proceed, rather than updating everything at once. Incremental refactoring minimizes disruption to the codebase and also reduces contributing and reviewing effort.  This refactoring could be something I could conduct at the PyCon India's sprint([proposal submitted](https://in.pycon.org/cfp/devsprint-2024/proposals/networkx-and-nx-parallel-sprint~dJ6Wl/)) this month. LMK your thoughts on this and then we can accordingly put a "sprint" and/or "good-first" label on this issue.   Thank you :)

title: Shortest path with weight=weight_function not uniquely identifying MultiEdges
body: ```py import networkx as nx  # Create a multidigraph G = nx.MultiDiGraph()  # Add edges with different weights G.add_edge(0, 1, weight=5, key=0) G.add_edge(0, 1, weight=2, key=1)  def f(u, v, d):     print(u,v,d)     return 1  # Find the shortest path shortest_path = nx.shortest_path(G, source=0, target=1, weight=f) #shortest_path = nx.shortest_path(G, source=0, target=1, weight='weight') path_length = nx.shortest_path_length(G, source=0, target=1, weight='weight')  print(f"Shortest path: {shortest_path}") print(f"Path length: {path_length}") print(f"Edge data: {G.get_edge_data(0, 1)}") ```  Shortest path (djikstra by default), works fine with multigraphs and a single scalar weight value, but when using a function for the weight, only passes u,v,dict key->data, which makes it impossible in the weight_function to distinguish which multiedge is currently selected.  ```py 0 1 {0: {'weight': 5}, 1: {'weight': 2}} 0 1 {0: {'weight': 5}, 1: {'weight': 2}} Shortest path: [0, 1] Path length: 2 Edge data: {0: {'weight': 5}, 1: {'weight': 2}} ```  i.e. this is the current output of the above code, while both multiedges are correctly traversed, they both get the same key->data dict, and thus it is not trivial to return the correct weight value.  A more reasonable behaviour would be to use the weight_function(u,v,k,d) or weight_function(u,v,{k:d}).

title: `algorithms.bridges.bridges()` does a redundant copy of graph
body: This is the code of the `bridges` function:  ```python def bridges(G, root=None):     multigraph = G.is_multigraph()     H = nx.Graph(G) if multigraph else G     chains = nx.chain_decomposition(H, root=root)     chain_edges = set(chain.from_iterable(chains))     H_copy = H.copy()     if root is not None:         H = H.subgraph(nx.node_connected_component(H, root)).copy()     for u, v in H.edges():         if (u, v) not in chain_edges and (v, u) not in chain_edges:             if multigraph and len(G[u][v]) > 1:                 continue             yield u, v ```  The statement in the middle:  ```python     H_copy = H.copy() ```  Seem to have no effect, because `H_copy` is not used anywhere else in this module, and therefore **can be removed**.  ### Current Behavior  Actually in addition to being redundant due to `H_copy` not used anywhere, presence of this statement makes extending the `networkx.Graph` class harder.  If you inherit from `networkx.Graph` and your class would have a constructor that requires some parameters to be provided, you wouldn't be able to use the `bridges()` function at all. Because this `.copy()` method has the following line:  ```python # Body of .copy() method G = self.__class__() ```  And for inheritors of `networkx.Graph` that have custom constructors `self.__class__()` raises `TypeError` on missing arguments.  ### Expected Behavior  There should be no redundant lines, and `bridges()` should work for inheritors as long as they don't override some dependent methods.  ### Steps to Reproduce  Set up for example this:  ```python class Map(nx.Graph):      def __init__(self: tp.Self, routes: tp.Iterable[str]) -> None:         super().__init__() ```  Initialize this object like `Map(routes=("a", "b"))` and try using `bridges()` with it.  ### Environment  Python version: 3.11 NetworkX version: 3.3

title: Add config option to disable the cache warning message, update warning to include instructions on how to disable
body: As discussed by @dschult , @eriknw , and @rlratzel at PyCon US 2024, the current behavior of warning users when they enable caching to inform them that changing graph attributes after the converted graph is cached will result in a stale cached value seems adequate for now and possibly longer-term. title: Can't replicate directed functionality of deprecated `random_tree`
body: The deprecated `random_tree` function supported the `create_using` kwarg to allow the creation of directed trees:  ```python >>> G = nx.random_tree(10, create_using=nx.DiGraph, seed=42) >>> G.edges OutEdgeView([(0, 6), (0, 4), (1, 5), (1, 8), (2, 1), (3, 7), (3, 2), (4, 3), (8, 9)]) ```  The `random_labeled_tree` function is the recommended replacement for the deprecated `random_tree` fn, but it doesn't support the `create_using` kwarg. AFAICT, the only way to replicate the current behavior of `random_tree` is to create a DiGraph from the generated edges manually:  ```python >>> H = nx.random_labeled_tree(10, seed=42)  # Undirected >>> DH = nx.DiGraph() >>> DH.add_edges_from(H) ```  I'm mostly just raising for visibility - I don't recall if this was an explicit decision to remove `create_using` support - @vigna . From a user perspective it'd be convenient to be able to replicate existing functionality with as little code modification as possible.

title: `compute_v_structures` output and docstring do not agree
body: ### Current Behavior The docstring of the method `compute_v_structures` in `dag.py` says  > Iterate through the graph to compute all v-structures. >  >     V-structures are triples in the directed graph where >     two parent nodes point to the same child and the two parent nodes >     are not adjacent. > ...  In particular, the part **_and the two parent nodes are not adjacent_** is what seems to disagree with the output of the iterator for a DAG. To my knowledge, in a DAG `G=(V, E)` two nodes `a,b` are adjacent if `(a,b) in E || (b,a) in E`:  ``` In [6]: import networkx as nx  In [7]: G = nx.DiGraph()    ...: G.add_edges_from([(2, 4), (5, 4), (2, 5)])    ...: list(nx.compute_v_structures(G)) Out[7]: [(2, 4, 5)]  In [8]: list(G.adjacency()) Out[8]: [(2, {4: {}, 5: {}}), (4, {}), (5, {4: {}})] ```  Clearly, 2 and 5 are adjacent, yet the function still returns (2,4,5) as a v-structure.  ### Expected Behavior  The test case above should return an empty list or the docstring should change its specification of v-structures.  ### Steps to Reproduce  Install `networkx >= 3.1` and run the above commands.  ### Environment  <!--- Please provide details about your local environment -->  Python version: 3.8 - 3.11 NetworkX version: 3.1 - 3.21

title: Follow-up to #7313 - replace explicit ref links to headers with automod
body: #7313 fixed many missing references in NX's `objects.inv` database by explicitly linking module names to section headings in the docstring.  Another pattern that could be considered is moving the autosummary's for those to the corresponding module docstrings and then using automod in the reference guide to automatically generate everything, and remove any possibility of collision of link names. title: Deprecate `reverse_cuthill_mckee_ordering`?
body: There are currently two functions in the `nx.utils.rcm` module: `cuthill_mckee_ordering` and `reverse_cuthill_mckee_ordering`. The former is a generator which yields nodes in rcm ordering; but the reversed version is a one-liner: `return reversed(list(cuthill_mckee_ordering(G, heuristic=heuristic)`.  The fact that the forward rcm is a generator whereas the reverse is not (instead returning an instantiated list) means that there is a (potentially) large difference in memory footprint[^1] between these two objects. This difference strikes me as worth resolving. One potential solution would be to deprecated the `reverse` version and recommend using `reversed` explicitly. Another possible solution would be to explicitly implement `reversed_cuthill_mckee_ordering` as a generator. This seems like a challenge, since I'm not sure that it would be possible to invert the ordering from a heuristic generically. However; if anyone has and ideas how this could be accomplished, it'd be interesting to see IMO!  [^1]: In practice I can't imagine this is a constraint that is hit too often, especially since the memory footprint of any graph of >10^6 nodes is likely to be far larger than it's node list.

title: Inconsistency in return type of `all_node_cuts`
body: I noticed this while reviewing docstrings in #7258.  From the documentation, it seems `all_node_cuts` is intended to return node sets. This is indeed the behavior for some graphs, e.g.  ```python >>> G = nx.path_graph(5) >>> list(nx.all_node_cuts(G)) [{1}, {2}, {3}] ```  However, for other input graphs, the returned values are sets of 2-tuples (which to me look suspiciously like edges). One example of this behavior is actually available in the docstring itself:  ```python >>> G = nx.grid_2d_graph(5, 5) >>> list(nx.all_node_cuts(G)) [{(3, 0), (4, 1)}, {(0, 3), (1, 4)}, {(3, 4), (4, 3)}, {(0, 1), (1, 0)}] ```  The sets in this last output don't appear to me to be interpretable as node cut-sets. Perhaps there's a missing edge-unpacking step somewhere in the algorithm?

title: `nonisomorphic_trees`  create argument
body: the `nonisomorphic_trees` graph generator has [an argument](https://github.com/networkx/networkx/blob/2da36864c5899cbc55fc98c96635390dd96d5f88/networkx/generators/nonisomorphic_trees.py#L16) named `create` which toggles whether graphs are returned as either nx.Graph instances, or adjacency matrices in list-of-list format.  From a quick review of this function, I'm wondering if it might not be worth deprecating this `create` argument. For one thing, it is very similar to `create_using=` which is ubiquitous among the graph generation functions and has a very different meaning! Also I'm not sure that returning adjacency matrices as `list` should even be an option - if anything I'd expect users to want adjacency matrices in a form more suitable for efficient computation, i.e. numpy arrays. The latter would be possible with something like `np.to_numpy_array(G) for G in nx.nonisomorphic_trees(order)`, so there is a straightforward way to get the (arguably more desirable) behavior after a deprecation.

title: Return type of `general_k_edge_subgraphs` is incorrect in docstring
body: In networkx 3.2.1, `general_k_edge_subgraphs` return type in docstring says this: ```     k_edge_subgraphs : a generator of nx.Graphs that are k-edge-subgraphs         Each k-edge-subgraph is a maximal set of nodes that defines a subgraph         of G that is k-edge-connected. ``` However, it actually _yields_ (not returns) _graphs_, not sets of nodes.

title: Docstring of `nonisomorphic_trees` should use `Yields`, not `Returns`

title: "dispatch" decorator needs documentation for contributors and readers of code
body: ### Current Behavior  Many of the NetworkX algorithm implementation functions are preceded by a decorator `@nx._dispatch` or variant. It is difficult for a person reading the algorithm, who just wants to understand how the Python code in the function behaves, to understand the behaviour of that decorator. How does it change the behaviour of the plain Python code in the function? How should the reader summarise in their mind the purpose of the "dispatch" decorator?  For example, a plain `@nx._dispatch` decorates [approximation algorithm `min_maximal_matching`](https://github.com/networkx/networkx/blob/1168afca385dab8cbda8be3aa479a22581e94988/networkx/algorithms/approximation/matching.py#L16C1-L18C52): ``` @nx._dispatch def min_maximal_matching(G):     r"""Returns the minimum maximal matching of G. ... ```  A `@nx._dispatch()` with kwarg decorates [algorithm `flow_hierarchy`](https://github.com/networkx/networkx/blob/1168afca385dab8cbda8be3aa479a22581e94988/networkx/algorithms/hierarchy.py#L9-L11) ``` @nx._dispatch(edge_attrs="weight") def flow_hierarchy(G, weight=None):     """Returns the flow hierarchy of a directed network. ... ``` ... and dozens more.
